blocks.html: The calm, balanced pictures of the High Renaissance and the stretched, restless figures of Mannerism gave way, around 1600, to a new style. Later critics called it Baroque. It lasted until about 1750 and spread from Rome across Catholic Europe, to the courts of Spain, France and Austria, and to the Americas.

Baroque artists wanted you to feel a scene, not only to admire it. Their tools: strong contrasts of light and dark, bodies caught in the middle of an action, diagonal compositions that rush into depth, rich color and texture, and spaces that seem to spill out toward the viewer. Painting, sculpture and architecture were often joined into one theatrical whole.
Baroque art (about 1600 to 1750) uses drama, motion, strong light and dark, and diagonals to pull the viewer into the scene. Its great patrons were the Catholic Church and powerful kings.

Context explains the style. The Catholic Church, answering the Protestant Reformation, called at the Council of Trent (1545 to 1563) for religious art that was clear and moving to ordinary people. Kings such as Louis XIV of France wanted art that showed their power. Both wanted art that worked on the viewer, and drama does that.

blocks.text: Looking closely: The Calling of Saint Matthew

blocks.name: ar-artwork

hotspots.label: The pointing hand
hotspots.text: Christ, half hidden behind Saint Peter, points across the room.

hotspots.label: The beam of light
hotspots.text: Light enters from the upper right and runs along the line of the hand, toward the table.

hotspots.label: Who is Matthew?
hotspots.text: Most scholars think Matthew is the bearded man pointing to himself; some have argued for the young man bent over the coins.

blocks.cap: Caravaggio, The Calling of Saint Matthew, 1599 to 1600. Contarelli Chapel, San Luigi dei Francesi, Rome.

blocks.html: Describe. Five men in the clothes of Caravaggio's own Rome sit at a table counting money in a bare room. Two figures enter at the right; the one in shadow points. Analyze. Almost everything is dark except a sharp diagonal of light from the upper right. The light follows the pointing hand across the wall to the faces at the table, so the light itself becomes the action. The moment is the instant before anyone moves. Interpret. The story (a tax collector called to follow Jesus) happens here and now, among ordinary people, and we watch from just across the table.

blocks.name: ar-compare
blocks.cap: High Renaissance (A) and Baroque (B): a calm, centered scene against a sudden diagonal moment.

blocks.title: Is it Baroque?
blocks.q: A painting shows a saint thrown backward as a beam of light strikes him, his horse rearing, the scene cut off at the edges. Which Baroque traits can you name?
steps: A dramatic moment, not a calm pose: motion.
A beam of light against darkness: strong contrast.
Figures cut off at the edges, as if the scene continues into our space: viewer involvement.
Together these point to the Baroque.
blocks.a: Motion, strong light and dark, and a scene that reaches toward the viewer.

blocks.html: People use "baroque" to mean just "fancy" or "overdecorated." Ornament is part of some Baroque buildings, but the style is about drama and involving the viewer. A plain, dark Caravaggio with no ornament at all is fully Baroque. Check for motion, contrast and a viewer drawn in, not for gold.

blocks.cap: The Baroque between Mannerism and the Rococo. The Dutch Golden Age overlaps it.

blocks.html: The word baroque began as an insult: eighteenth-century critics used it for art they found strange and overdone. It may come from the Portuguese barroco, a misshapen pearl, though the origin is debated. Today it is a neutral name for the period.

blocks.html: Michelangelo Merisi da Caravaggio (1571 to 1610) came to Rome from Lombardy in the early 1590s and changed European painting within a few years. In What Makes Art Baroque you met his Calling of Saint Matthew. Here we look at how he made light do the storytelling.

Painters had long modeled forms with light and shadow, a method called chiaroscuro (Italian for "light-dark"). Caravaggio pushed it to an extreme: most of the picture sinks into deep shadow, and a single hard light picks out faces, hands and a few objects. This extreme form is called tenebrism, from the Italian tenebroso, "dark, murky." He also painted saints and apostles as ordinary-looking people, with lined faces, dirty feet and torn sleeves, which some patrons found shocking and many viewers found moving.
Tenebrism is chiaroscuro at its extreme: deep darkness with a sharp, focused light. Caravaggio used it, with ordinary-looking models, to make religious stories feel immediate.

A spotlight works like a stage. When almost everything is dark, the eye goes straight to what the light touches, so the painter controls exactly where you look and in what order. Caravaggio painted from posed models, lit from one side, and the strong light makes the figures look solid enough to touch.

blocks.text: Looking closely: The Supper at Emmaus

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Caravaggio, The Supper at Emmaus, 1601. National Gallery, London.

blocks.html: Describe. At an inn table, the risen Christ blesses bread. Two disciples react: one grips the arms of his chair, the other flings his arms wide. The innkeeper stands, puzzled. Analyze. Light from the upper left falls on the faces and the white cloth; the background is a dark brown wall. The outflung arms push forward and back in depth, and the fruit basket teeters at the very edge of the table, as if it could fall into our space. Interpret. This is the moment of recognition in the story, when the disciples realize who their companion is; the reaching gestures and the basket pull us into that moment.

blocks.name: ar-compose
blocks.cap: The arms and the table edge make strong diagonals; the lit face of Christ is the focal point.

blocks.html: People mix up chiaroscuro and tenebrism. Chiaroscuro is any modeling with light and dark, and Leonardo used it softly. Tenebrism is its extreme: most of the picture in deep shadow, with a hard, narrow light. Check: if large parts of the picture are nearly black and the light is a sharp spotlight, it is tenebrism.

blocks.title: Chiaroscuro or tenebrism?
blocks.q: A portrait shows a face gently turning from light into soft shadow against a mid-gray background. Is that tenebrism?
steps: There is modeling from light to shadow, so it uses chiaroscuro.
The shadows are soft and the background is mid-gray, not deep darkness.
There is no sharp spotlight against near-black.
blocks.a: No. It is chiaroscuro, but not tenebrism.

blocks.html: Caravaggio's style spread fast. His followers, the Caravaggisti, carried tenebrism to Naples, Spain, France and Utrecht in the Dutch Republic. You will meet one of the greatest of them, Artemisia Gentileschi, in the next lesson, and his influence again in Velázquez and Rembrandt.

Caravaggio's life was stormy: he was often in trouble with the law and fled Rome in 1606. Historians still piece together his last years from scattered records. His paintings, not his legend, are what changed art.

blocks.html: Artemisia Gentileschi (1593 to about 1656) was the daughter of the painter Orazio Gentileschi, a friend and follower of Caravaggio. She trained in her father's studio in Rome, because women were not admitted to the usual apprenticeships, and became one of the most sought-after painters of her century.

Her career took her from Rome to Florence, back to Rome, to Venice, to Naples and to London. In Florence, on July 19, 1616, she became the first woman admitted to the Accademia delle Arti del Disegno (the Academy of the Arts of Drawing), founded in 1563 as the first academy of art. Membership let her sign contracts and buy materials in her own name. Her patrons included the Medici family of Florence and King Charles I of England.
Artemisia Gentileschi, a follower of Caravaggio's dramatic style, was the first woman admitted to Florence's Academy of the Arts of Drawing (1616) and painted for princes and kings across Europe.

Women artists were rare because the system shut them out: they could not join most workshops, travel freely or study from life in academies. The women who succeeded, like Gentileschi, usually trained with an artist father. Her membership in the academy mattered because it gave her a legal and professional standing most women lacked.

blocks.text: Looking closely: Self-Portrait as the Allegory of Painting

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Artemisia Gentileschi, Self-Portrait as the Allegory of Painting, about 1638 to 1639. Royal Collection, United Kingdom.

blocks.html: Describe. A woman in a green dress leans toward an unseen canvas, brush raised in one hand and palette in the other. A gold chain with a small mask pendant hangs at her neck, and strands of her dark hair fall loose. Analyze. Her body makes a strong diagonal from the lower right to the raised arm at the upper left. Light falls on her face, arm and sleeve; the background is plain brown. The pose is hard to see in a mirror, which shows how much skill it took. Interpret. Cesare Ripa's Iconologia (1593), a handbook of symbols, described Painting as a woman with a gold chain and mask pendant and untidy hair. Gentileschi painted herself as that figure, so she is both the artist at work and Painting itself.

blocks.title: Reading an allegory
blocks.q: An allegory uses a figure to stand for an idea. How do we know this woman stands for Painting?
steps: She holds a brush and palette and works at a canvas.
She wears a gold chain with a mask, a sign of imitation, which handbooks gave to the figure of Painting.
Her untidy hair matches the same handbook, which linked it to the artist's inspired, busy mind.
blocks.a: Her tools and her attributes (chain, mask, loose hair) match the traditional figure of Painting.

blocks.html: People think there were no women artists before modern times. Many were famous in their own day: Sofonisba Anguissola (about 1532 to 1625) was a court painter in Spain; Artemisia Gentileschi worked for kings; Judith Leyster ran her own workshop in Haarlem; Rachel Ruysch was a court painter in Düsseldorf. Their names were often forgotten later, and some of their works were credited to men.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Sofonisba Anguissola, The Chess Game, 1555. National Museum, Poznań. Her sisters play chess while a servant watches.

blocks.html: Most scholars accept the Allegory of Painting as a self-portrait, painted around the time she worked in London; a few have questioned the identification. Many of Gentileschi's best-known works show violent biblical stories, which this course leaves aside. Her portraits and allegories show her skill just as well.

blocks.html: Gian Lorenzo Bernini (1598 to 1680) was a sculptor, architect and stage designer who worked for a series of popes, above all Urban VIII and Alexander VII. More than anyone, he gave Baroque Rome its look. Rome was the center of the Catholic Church, and the popes wanted the city to welcome pilgrims and show the Church's confidence after the Reformation (see What Makes Art Baroque).

blocks.text: Looking closely: the colonnade of St. Peter's Square

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Gian Lorenzo Bernini, Colonnade of St. Peter's Square, 1656 to 1667. Vatican City.

blocks.html: Describe. In front of St. Peter's Basilica, two great curved arms of columns enclose an oval piazza. The colonnades have 284 Doric columns in four rows, built of travertine stone, with 140 statues of saints along the top. Analyze. Walk in and the curving rows seem to close around you; walk along them and the columns line up and open again, so the space changes as you move. The oval sets the basilica at the end of a grand, theatrical approach. Interpret. Bernini himself compared the arms to the motherly arms of the Church, embracing the faithful who arrived.

blocks.name: ar-map
blocks.cap: Rome and the Vatican, with the other Baroque centers of this unit.

blocks.html: Bernini shaped Baroque Rome as sculptor and architect. His colonnade for St. Peter's Square (1656 to 1667) wraps the piazza like open arms.

Bernini's great rival, Francesco Borromini (1599 to 1667), built the small church of San Carlo alle Quattro Fontane (1638 to 1641; façade finished 1677). Its walls swing in and out in waves, and its oval dome is covered in a honeycomb of crosses, octagons and hexagons (coffers) that shrink toward the lantern at the top, so the dome looks taller than it is.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Francesco Borromini, the oval dome of San Carlo alle Quattro Fontane, Rome, 1638 to 1641.

blocks.html: A Renaissance church is built from clear, separate units: squares, circles, straight walls. Borromini and Bernini made the wall itself bend. Convex and concave curves push and pull against each other, and light from hidden windows falls from above. The building seems to move, which is the Baroque goal of involving the viewer turned into stone.

People think Baroque buildings are just Renaissance ones with more ornament. Check the plan and the walls: Renaissance buildings use flat walls and simple shapes; Baroque architects bent walls into curves, used ovals, and staged light, so the space seems to move as you walk.

blocks.title: Renaissance or Baroque?
blocks.q: A church façade curves in at the sides and bulges out in the middle, with deep shadows between its columns. Which style is it, and why?
steps: The façade is not flat: it curves in and out.
Columns cast deep shadows, giving strong light and dark.
A wall that seems to move is a Baroque idea.
blocks.a: Baroque: the curving, moving wall and strong contrasts.

blocks.html: Bernini was a sculptor first. His marble figures in Roman churches catch people mid-action, with fluttering drapery and open mouths, as if the stone were alive. He also designed fountains, tombs and the great bronze canopy over the high altar of St. Peter's.

blocks.html: Diego Velázquez (1599 to 1660) trained in Seville, where he painted kitchen scenes with strong Caravaggio-like light. In 1623 he became painter to King Philip IV in Madrid and stayed at court for the rest of his life. Two trips to Italy loosened his brushwork: up close his paintings are quick, separate strokes; from a few steps back they turn into silk, lace and skin.

blocks.name: ar-artwork

hotspots.label: The painter
hotspots.text: Velázquez stands at a huge canvas, brush in hand, looking out at us.

hotspots.label: The mirror
hotspots.text: A small mirror on the back wall reflects King Philip IV and Queen Mariana.

hotspots.label: The princess
hotspots.text: The five-year-old Infanta Margarita Teresa, lit by light from the right.

hotspots.label: The doorway
hotspots.text: The queen's chamberlain pauses on the stairs in a bright doorway.

blocks.cap: Diego Velázquez, Las Meninas, 1656. Museo del Prado, Madrid.

blocks.html: Describe. In a tall room of the royal palace in Madrid, the five-year-old princess Margarita Teresa stands at the center, with two maids of honor (the meninas), two court dwarfs, a dog, a chaperone and a guard. At the left, Velázquez himself stands at a huge canvas whose front we cannot see. A small mirror on the back wall shows the king and queen, and a man pauses in a lit doorway. Analyze. The light from windows at the right falls on the princess, the focal point. The upper half of the canvas is dark and empty, which pushes the figures down and forward. The space goes deep, back to the doorway. Several figures look straight out, at us. Interpret. If the mirror reflects the king and queen, they stand where we stand. The picture turns the viewer into part of the scene.
Velázquez, court painter to Philip IV, painted Las Meninas (1656), a picture about looking: the painter, the princess and a mirror all look out toward the place where we stand.

Velázquez stood close to the king and wanted painting to be seen as a noble, intellectual art, not a craft. Las Meninas shows the painter at work beside the royal family, in the palace, as an equal participant. Its puzzles make the viewer think about how a painting is made and seen.

People think Las Meninas is a simple group portrait. Look again: we cannot see what Velázquez is painting, and the mirror may reflect the king and queen standing in our place, or the painting on his canvas. Scholars have debated who is being painted, and where the viewer stands, for centuries. Say what you see, then give the possibilities.

blocks.title: Where is the king?
blocks.q: The mirror on the back wall shows King Philip IV and Queen Mariana. Name two possible explanations.
steps: A mirror shows what is in front of it.
So the king and queen may be standing in front of the scene, where the viewer is, posing for Velázquez.
Or the mirror may reflect the front of the big canvas, on which Velázquez is painting them.
The painting does not settle it, and scholars still disagree.
blocks.a: They may stand in our place, or the mirror may show the canvas; the question is still debated.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Diego Velázquez, Juan de Pareja, 1650. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York.

blocks.html: In Rome in 1650 Velázquez painted Juan de Pareja, his assistant, who was enslaved in his household. That year Velázquez signed a document promising Pareja his freedom after four more years of service; Pareja was freed in 1654 and became a painter in his own right. The portrait was shown in Rome to great praise. Its gray-green palette, the few quick strokes of the lace collar and the direct gaze show Velázquez's late, free style.

Philip IV's court was one of the great patrons of the age; much of its collection is now in the Prado. Velázquez also painted the king, the royal children and members of the court, including court dwarfs, with the same dignity.

blocks.html: In the Catholic southern Netherlands (Flanders, today Belgium), the city of Antwerp had its own Baroque. Its leader was Peter Paul Rubens (1577 to 1640). After eight years in Italy, where he studied ancient sculpture and the paintings of Titian and Michelangelo, he settled in Antwerp in 1608. He was also a scholar and a diplomat who carried messages between the courts of Spain and England, and was knighted by both kings.

Rubens painted with energy: twisting bodies, swirling drapery, warm, glowing skin and rich reds and golds. He ran one of the largest workshops in Europe, which turned out altarpieces, ceiling paintings, portraits and designs for tapestries and book illustrations.

blocks.text: Looking closely: Le Chapeau de Paille

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Peter Paul Rubens, Le Chapeau de Paille, about 1622 to 1625. National Gallery, London.

blocks.html: Describe. A young woman, probably Susanna Lunden, the sister of Rubens's second wife, stands with arms folded under a wide black hat with feathers, against a bright blue sky. Analyze. She is painted outdoors in daylight, and the hat casts a shadow over her eyes, yet her face glows with light reflected from the sky and from below. The red sleeves and the deep blue sky are strong complements. Interpret. It is an intimate portrait of someone in the painter's family, and a display of how light behaves out of doors, long before the Impressionists made that their subject.
Rubens ran a huge Antwerp workshop and painted with energetic color and movement. His most gifted assistant, Anthony van Dyck, became court painter to Charles I of England.

Big commissions such as altarpieces and palace ceilings needed many hands. In Rubens's workshop the master made the design, often an oil sketch; trained assistants and specialists painted large parts; then Rubens finished and corrected the work. Prices could depend on how much of a painting he did himself.

People think a "Rubens" was painted by Rubens alone. Large works came from his workshop: Rubens designed them and painted key parts, assistants did much of the rest, and specialists sometimes added animals, flowers or landscapes. Museums label works "Rubens and workshop" when the evidence shows this.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Anthony van Dyck, Charles I at the Hunt, about 1635. Louvre, Paris.

blocks.html: Anthony van Dyck (1599 to 1641) was Rubens's most gifted assistant. In 1632 he settled in London as painter to King Charles I, who knighted him. In Charles I at the Hunt, the king has dismounted and stands at ease, hand on hip, in a landscape, while a groom holds his horse. The low viewpoint makes him seem tall; his relaxed pose and silver silk suggest a gentleman as well as a king. Van Dyck's elegant portraits set the pattern for British portraiture for more than a century (see The Grand Manner Portrait).

blocks.title: Master or workshop?
blocks.q: A huge altarpiece by Rubens has a brilliantly painted central figure, while some background figures look stiffer. What might explain this?
steps: Large works were made by Rubens's workshop.
Rubens often painted the most important parts himself.
Assistants may have painted the rest from his design.
blocks.a: The difference may show the master's hand and his assistants' hands in one work.

blocks.cap: Two Flemish Baroque portraits: Rubens (A) and his assistant Van Dyck (B).

blocks.html: Baroque architecture began in Rome with Bernini and Borromini and spread to palaces and churches all over Europe. Kings borrowed the style for the same reason the popes used it: grand, theatrical spaces impress visitors and announce power.

The Palace of Versailles, about 20 kilometers southwest of Paris, began as a modest hunting lodge built for King Louis XIII around 1623. From the early 1660s his son, Louis XIV, enlarged it again and again with the architects Louis Le Vau and later Jules Hardouin-Mansart, the painter Charles Le Brun and the garden designer André Le Nôtre. In 1682 Louis moved his court and government there. The Hall of Mirrors (1678 to 1684) is 73 meters long, with 357 mirrors facing tall windows onto the gardens. The gardens stretch out along straight axes, with fountains, clipped hedges and a long canal, so that nature itself seems to obey the king.

Baroque palaces and churches used scale, axis and dazzling interiors to show power. Versailles grew from a royal hunting lodge into Louis XIV's palace from the 1660s; St. Paul's Cathedral in London was rebuilt by Christopher Wren from 1675 to 1710.

A palace was a political tool. At Versailles the nobles of France lived under the king's eye, taking part in daily ceremonies around him, instead of plotting in their own castles. Every vista, painted ceiling and garden path led back to Louis, the "Sun King."

People think Versailles was always a palace. It began as a royal hunting lodge for Louis XIII (around 1623). Louis XIV transformed it in several building campaigns from the 1660s to about 1710. When you date a building, ask whether it was built at once or grew over time.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: The west front of St. Paul's Cathedral, London, in an eighteenth-century engraving. Christopher Wren, 1675 to 1710.

blocks.html: Describe. The Great Fire of London in 1666 destroyed the medieval cathedral. Christopher Wren, a scientist turned architect, designed the new one. The west front has two stories of paired columns, two towers, and above them a great dome on a ring of columns. Analyze. The towers, with their curving, layered tops, show Borromini's influence; the calm paired columns and the dome on its drum recall Renaissance models such as Bramante and Michelangelo's St. Peter's. The building rises 111 meters (365 feet) to the cross on top of the dome. Interpret. This is an English Baroque, more restrained than Rome's, built for a Protestant city that wanted grandeur without excess.

blocks.name: ar-arch
blocks.cap: How a dome sits on a square space: Wren's dome, like St. Peter's, rests on a drum above the crossing.

blocks.title: How do we date it?
blocks.q: An old engraving of St. Paul's shows the finished dome. Could the engraving be from 1680?
steps: Wren began building in 1675.
The cathedral was finished in 1710, and the dome was among the last parts completed.
An engraving of the finished dome must be from about 1710 or later, unless it copies a design drawing.
blocks.a: Probably not: a view of the finished building dates from about 1710 or later.

blocks.html: In the 1600s the northern Netherlands broke away from Spanish rule and formed the Dutch Republic. It was small, but trade made it one of the richest places in Europe. Its art looked very different from the Baroque of Rome and Madrid, because the buyers were different.

Most Dutch churches were Calvinist Protestant, and they did not use religious paintings in worship. There was no great royal court and few grand palaces. Instead, merchants, shopkeepers, craftsmen and city officials bought pictures for their homes. Visitors from abroad were struck by how many paintings ordinary Dutch houses held.

With few church or royal commissions and many middle-class buyers, Dutch painters of the 1600s made portraits, landscapes, still lifes and genre scenes (everyday life), often painted first and sold on the open market.

Selling to strangers changes how art is made. A painter who waits for a commission paints what a patron orders. A painter who sells through a dealer, a shop or a fair paints what many buyers might want, in sizes that fit a house, and often specializes so buyers know what they are getting. That is why Dutch painters were specialists: one painted seascapes, another flowers, another tavern scenes, another church interiors.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Johannes Vermeer, The Milkmaid, about 1660. Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam.

blocks.html: Describe. A kitchen maid in a yellow bodice and blue apron pours milk into a bowl, with bread on a table by a window. Analyze. Light from the left window falls on her and on the bread; the wall behind is pale and bare, so she stands out. Interpret. A picture of household work, painted for sale, became a picture of quiet attention. It is the kind of everyday subject the Dutch market wanted, raised to great art. You will look at it closely in Vermeer.

People think painters always worked on commission. Many Dutch artists painted first and then sold through dealers, shops, auctions, lotteries and fairs. Portraits and some large works were still commissioned, so check: was the work ordered by someone, or made to sell?

blocks.title: Commission or market?
blocks.q: A small still life of fish and a jug, one of many similar works by the same painter, was found in a dealer's inventory in 1650. Was it more likely commissioned or made for the market?
steps: It is small, fits a home, and has a common subject.
The painter made many similar works, a sign of specializing for buyers.
It sat in a dealer's stock, waiting to sell.
blocks.a: Made for the market.

blocks.html: Painters were organized in the Guild of Saint Luke of each city, which controlled who could sell paintings and take pupils. The same market drove other Dutch passions, including flowers: in 1636 and 1637 prices for rare tulip bulbs soared and then collapsed, an episode called tulip mania.
Not everything was for sale. Rich citizens still commissioned portraits, and civic groups such as militia companies ordered big group portraits for their halls, like Rembrandt's Night Watch.

Rembrandt van Rijn (1606 to 1669) was born in Leiden and moved to Amsterdam in the early 1630s, where he became the city's leading portrait painter. He painted, drew and etched: portraits, Bible stories, landscapes and himself. Like Caravaggio, he used strong light and dark, but his shadows are warm and full of half-seen detail.

blocks.name: ar-artwork

hotspots.label: The captain
hotspots.text: Captain Frans Banninck Cocq, in black with a red sash, steps forward and gives an order.

hotspots.label: The lieutenant
hotspots.text: Lieutenant Willem van Ruytenburch, in pale yellow. The captain's hand casts a shadow on his coat.

hotspots.label: The girl in gold
hotspots.text: A girl lit as brightly as the officers carries the company's emblems, including a bird's claws, a sign of the musketeers.

hotspots.label: The drummer
hotspots.text: A drummer beats the call to march.

blocks.cap: Rembrandt van Rijn, The Night Watch, 1642. Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam.

blocks.html: Describe. A militia company, the citizen guards of one district of Amsterdam, pours out from under an archway. The captain in black and the lieutenant in pale yellow stride toward us; around them men load and raise muskets, a banner is unfurled, a dog barks and a drummer beats the drum. Analyze. Earlier group portraits lined members up in rows, each face equally clear. Rembrandt made a scene of motion instead: diagonals of spears and muskets, bright light on the two officers and on a girl in gold, and deep shadow elsewhere. Interpret. It is a portrait of the company, paid for by its members, and a picture of civic pride: Amsterdam's citizens ready to defend their city.
Rembrandt turned the group portrait into a scene full of motion and light in The Night Watch (1642), and painted searching self-portraits throughout his life.

People think The Night Watch is a night scene. It is set in daylight. Layers of varnish and dirt darkened it, and the nickname appears in records only in 1797. Cleaning has brought back much of its light. The real title names the company: The Militia Company of District II under the Command of Captain Frans Banninck Cocq.

A group portrait had to please every member who paid, and each wanted a clear likeness. Rembrandt took a risk by putting some faces in shadow to make a living scene. The painting was also cut down on all sides in 1715 so that it would fit a wall in Amsterdam's town hall, which is why some figures are cropped at the edge.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Rembrandt van Rijn, Self-Portrait, 1659. National Gallery of Art, Washington.

blocks.html: Rembrandt made more than eighty self-portraits in paintings, etchings and drawings, more than any major artist before him. In this one, painted at 53, three years after his bankruptcy, he looks straight at us under a dark beret. The face is built of thick, worked paint that catches the light; the clothes melt into brown shadow. The portrait does not flatter. It records age and experience with honesty.

blocks.title: Why the nickname?
blocks.q: A visitor in 1800 called the painting "The Night Watch." Why might it have looked like night to her?
steps: The scene is set in daylight, but large areas are in shadow.
Old varnish turns yellow-brown and darkens with time and dirt.
Under that darkened varnish, the daylight scene looked like night.
blocks.a: Darkened varnish and Rembrandt's deep shadows made a daylight scene look like night.

blocks.html: Johannes Vermeer (1632 to 1675) spent his whole life in Delft. He painted slowly; only about 34 to 36 paintings are accepted as his today. Most show one or two people in a quiet room, lit from a window on the left. His buyers were local, and he was almost forgotten for two centuries until a French critic, Théophile Thoré-Bürger, championed him in the 1860s. Vermeer is the most famous painter of the Dutch market's everyday subjects.

blocks.name: ar-artwork

hotspots.label: The stream of milk
hotspots.text: A thin, steady stream: the one moving thing in a still room.

hotspots.label: Dots of light
hotspots.text: Small dabs of pale paint make the crust of the bread sparkle.

hotspots.label: The window
hotspots.text: Light comes from the left, through a window with a broken pane.

hotspots.label: Ultramarine
hotspots.text: The blue of the apron is natural ultramarine, a costly pigment made from lapis lazuli.

blocks.cap: Johannes Vermeer, The Milkmaid, about 1660. Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam.

blocks.html: Describe. A sturdy kitchen maid pours milk from a jug into a bowl. On the table are bread, a basket and a blue jug; on the wall, a basket and a brass pail; on the floor, a foot warmer and a row of tiles. Analyze. Light from the window falls across her face, her yellow bodice and the bread. Vermeer made the bread and basket glitter with tiny dots of light, a technique called pointillé. The colors are few and strong: yellow, blue and red, against a pale wall. Her arms and the table edge lead to the stream of milk. Interpret. Simple work is shown with care and dignity. Every object is still except the milk, and the scene feels calm and timeless.
Vermeer of Delft painted calm rooms lit from a side window, with dots of light (pointillé) and costly natural ultramarine, as in The Milkmaid (about 1660).

Ultramarine was made by grinding lapis lazuli, a stone mined in Afghanistan, and it cost more than gold by weight. Vermeer used it generously, even mixed into shadows, which gives his blues and his cool daylight their depth. Using such a pigment on a picture of a maid tells us how seriously he took the subject.

People state as fact that Vermeer traced an image from a camera obscura (a darkened box or room in which a lens projects a picture). Some scholars think he used one, pointing to effects like the glittering highlights and sharp perspective; others disagree. There is no direct evidence, such as a document or traced lines. Say "may have used," not "used."

blocks.name: ar-compare
blocks.cap: Two more Vermeers: Girl with a Pearl Earring (A), a tronie, and View of Delft (B).

blocks.html: Girl with a Pearl Earring (about 1665) is not a portrait of a known person. It is a tronie, a Dutch term for a study of a face, here in an exotic turban. View of Delft (about 1660 to 1661) shows his city across the water under a wide, cloudy sky.

blocks.title: Is it a portrait?
blocks.q: A museum label calls Girl with a Pearl Earring a tronie. Does that mean we know who the sitter was?
steps: A tronie is a study of a face, often in costume.
It was painted to sell as a character study, not ordered by a sitter.
So it does not record a particular person, and her identity is unknown.
blocks.a: No: a tronie is a character study, and the sitter is unknown.

blocks.html: Dating is debated. The Rijksmuseum dates The Milkmaid about 1660; some scholars place it a little earlier, about 1657 to 1658. Vermeer rarely dated his paintings, so their order is worked out from style and technical study.

blocks.html: Judith Leyster (1609 to 1660) grew up in Haarlem, the daughter of a cloth worker turned brewer, who named his brewery De Leyster (the lodestar) and took the name for the family. In 1633, at 24, she became a master in Haarlem's Guild of Saint Luke, one of the first women to do so. As a master she could sell her work, run a workshop and take pupils. She painted lively genre scenes of music-making and merry company, portraits and a few still lifes.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Judith Leyster, Self-Portrait, about 1630. National Gallery of Art, Washington.

blocks.html: Describe. Leyster turns from her easel toward us, smiling, lips parted as if about to speak. She holds a brush near a canvas on which a laughing violin player is taking shape, and a palette and a fistful of brushes in her other hand. She wears a fine dress with a wide lace collar. Analyze. The pose is relaxed and turning, the brushwork quick and loose, especially in the collar and the fiddler. Light from the left falls on her face, hand and brush. Interpret. Her clothes are far too fine for painting in, so this is a picture meant to sell her skill: a successful artist who can paint people laughing, music and lace, all in one canvas. Technical images show she first painted a different picture on the easel, a woman's figure, and changed it to the fiddler.

Judith Leyster, a master in Haarlem's painters' guild from 1633, painted lively genre scenes and a famous self-portrait at her easel (about 1630). For two centuries some of her works were sold as Frans Hals's.

Genre scenes sold well on the Dutch market. Leyster's merry musicians and drinkers, painted with the loose, sketchy strokes popular in Haarlem, looked like the work of the city's most famous painter, Frans Hals. That likeness, and the habit of crediting good paintings to famous men, is how her name was lost.

People think Leyster's works were by Frans Hals. Some of them were sold under Hals's name for two centuries. In 1893, the art historian Cornelis Hofstede de Groot found her monogram, the letters JL joined with a star (a pun on her name, "lodestar"), on paintings that had been sold as works by Hals. Other works have been restored to her since. Check signatures and monograms before trusting an old attribution.

blocks.title: Reading a monogram
blocks.q: A painting sold as a Frans Hals has a small mark: the letters J and L joined, with a star. What does that suggest?
steps: Hals signed with his own initials, FH.
J and L with a star is Judith Leyster's monogram; her name means "lodestar."
The mark suggests the painting is Leyster's, wrongly credited to Hals.
blocks.a: It is probably by Judith Leyster.

blocks.html: Genre scenes could be funny, rowdy or quiet, and many carry a light moral: a drinker who has had too much, a lute player tuning up for love, children at play. Viewers then enjoyed spotting these meanings, but scholars warn against reading every object as a hidden symbol.

blocks.html: Two genres flourished on the Dutch market: landscapes of the flat, watery country, and still lifes of flowers, food and fine things. Both look like plain records of what was there. Both were carefully composed.

blocks.text: Looking closely: The Windmill at Wijk bij Duurstede

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Jacob van Ruisdael, The Windmill at Wijk bij Duurstede, about 1668 to 1670. Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam.

blocks.html: Describe. A tall, round stone windmill rises above a riverbank, with a few small figures, a sailboat and the roofs of a town. Most of the canvas is sky, heavy with clouds. Analyze. The horizon is set very low, so the sky fills about two-thirds of the picture. The mill, seen from below, stands dark against bright clouds, and a band of sunlight crosses the middle ground. Interpret. Jacob van Ruisdael (about 1628 to 1682) made a portrait of the Dutch land: water, wind and a mill that turns wind into work. Viewers also read the weather as feeling, a sense of grandeur in an ordinary place.

Dutch painters made landscapes of their flat land and huge skies (Jacob van Ruisdael) and still lifes of flowers, food and objects (Rachel Ruysch, Pieter Claesz); vanitas still lifes reminded viewers that life is short.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Pieter Claesz, Vanitas Still Life, 1630. Mauritshuis, The Hague.

blocks.html: A vanitas (Latin for "emptiness," from a Bible verse about the vanity of all things) is a still life whose objects warn that life is short: a skull, a candle snuffed out, a watch, books, an overturned glass. Pieter Claesz (about 1597 to 1660) painted this one in browns, grays and greens, with a soft light that shows each texture: bone, paper, brass, glass. The objects are beautiful, and that is the point: even beautiful things pass.

Still lifes let painters show off their skill at textures, and they let buyers own something precious, even rare flowers, in paint. They also carried meanings that a Protestant household could hang on its wall: thoughts about time and death, and the gifts of trade and nature, without a religious scene.

People think a flower still life shows one real bouquet. Painters combined flowers that bloom in different seasons, spring tulips with summer roses, painted from separate studies over months. Rachel Ruysch (1664 to 1750), the most famous flower painter of her day and court painter in Düsseldorf from 1708, built her bouquets this way. Check: would all these flowers bloom at the same time?

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Rachel Ruysch, Still Life with Flowers in a Glass Vase, about 1690 to 1720. Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam.

blocks.title: A real bouquet?
blocks.q: A painting shows tulips (spring), roses (early summer) and a sunflower-like marigold (late summer) all in full bloom. Was it painted from one bouquet?
steps: Tulips bloom in spring; these roses in early summer; marigolds late in the season.
They could not all be fresh in one vase at once in the 1600s.
The painter combined separate studies into one composed bouquet.
blocks.a: No: it combines flowers from different seasons.

blocks.html: After Louis XIV died in 1715, French nobles moved from the formal halls of Versailles back to their town houses in Paris. They wanted smaller, lighter rooms for conversation, music and cards. A new style grew up there in the 1720s and spread across Europe: the Rococo (about 1720 to 1780). The name comes from the French rocaille, the shell and rock work used in garden grottoes, whose curling forms show up everywhere in its ornament.

Rococo rooms have pale walls, gilded curling frames, mirrors and delicate plaster scrolls; furniture has curved legs. Paintings use pastel colors (rose, sky blue, cream, pale green), soft light and graceful figures at leisure: parties in parks, music and courtship, elegant portraits. The painter Antoine Watteau (1684 to 1721) invented a whole type of picture, the fête galante, showing elegant couples in park settings.

Rococo (about 1720 to 1780) is light, elegant and playful: pastel color, small scale, curving ornament and scenes of graceful leisure. Élisabeth Vigée Le Brun painted Queen Marie Antoinette in this elegant spirit.

Style follows use. Baroque palaces were built to impress crowds and announce power. Rococo rooms were built for small groups of friends, so the scale shrank, the colors lightened and the mood relaxed. Art moved from public statements to private pleasure.

blocks.text: Looking closely: Marie Antoinette with a Rose

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Élisabeth Vigée Le Brun, Marie Antoinette with a Rose, 1783. Palace of Versailles.

blocks.html: Describe. The queen of France, in a blue-gray silk gown trimmed with lace, holds out a pink rose. Her powdered hair is piled high and topped with feathers; behind her is a dark, leafy garden. Analyze. The soft, cool blue and silver of the silk shine against the dark ground. Her face is smooth and idealized, the pose easy and graceful; her body turns one way, her head the other. Interpret. It is a royal portrait without throne or crown, showing the queen as gracious and gentle. Vigée Le Brun (1755 to 1842) painted it to replace an earlier 1783 portrait of the queen in a simple muslin dress, which critics thought too informal for a queen.

blocks.name: ar-compare
blocks.cap: Rococo (A) against Baroque (B): pastel silk and grace against deep shadow and drama.

blocks.html: People think Rococo is a heavier Baroque. It is lighter: pastel instead of deep color, small rooms instead of great halls, delicate curves instead of massive ones, play instead of grandeur. Check the color and scale first.

blocks.title: Baroque or Rococo?
blocks.q: A painting shows a young couple on a swing-seat in a park, in pale pinks and greens, with soft, feathery trees. Which style is it, and why?
steps: Pastel colors and soft light, not deep shadows.
The subject is elegant leisure and courtship, not drama.
The scale and mood are light and playful.
blocks.a: Rococo.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Élisabeth Vigée Le Brun, Self-Portrait in a Straw Hat, after 1782. National Gallery, London.

blocks.html: Vigée Le Brun saw Rubens's Le Chapeau de Paille in Antwerp in 1782 and painted her own version, with herself outdoors in a feathered hat, palette in hand. She was one of the most successful portraitists in Europe and painted the queen many times. After the French Revolution began in 1789, she left France and worked in Italy, Austria and Russia for twelve years.

blocks.html: Not all eighteenth-century painting was Rococo elegance. Two very different painters show other sides of the century: a Parisian who painted kitchens and children with quiet seriousness, and a Venetian who painted his city for tourists.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Jean-Siméon Chardin, Soap Bubbles, about 1733 to 1734. National Gallery of Art, Washington (other versions in New York and Los Angeles).

blocks.html: Describe. A young man leans on a stone window ledge and blows a bubble through a straw; a small child peeps over the ledge to watch. A glass of soapy water stands beside him, and a vine hangs above. Analyze. The colors are soft browns, grays and greens, and the light is gentle. The bubble, almost transparent, is the center of attention: everything in the picture, including the child's eyes, leads to it. Interpret. A bubble lasts a moment, so viewers of the time could read it as a reminder that life is brief, like the Dutch vanitas. It is also simply a moment of concentration, painted with great care.

Jean-Siméon Chardin (1699 to 1779) was admitted to the French Royal Academy in 1728 as a painter of still life, a low-ranked genre. He painted copper pots, fruit, servants at work and children playing, with soft, grainy paint. He made several versions of popular works like this one, for different buyers.
Chardin painted quiet kitchens, still lifes and children at play with soft color and seriousness; Canaletto painted precise-looking views of Venice (vedute) for travelers on the Grand Tour.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Canaletto, The Square of Saint Mark's, Venice, 1742 to 1744. National Gallery of Art, Washington.

blocks.html: Wealthy young Englishmen finished their education with the Grand Tour, a long journey through France and Italy to see ancient ruins and Renaissance art. They wanted souvenirs. Giovanni Antonio Canal, called Canaletto (1697 to 1768), sold them vedute, "views" of Venice, often through the British consul Joseph Smith. In The Square of Saint Mark's the basilica's domes and the Doge's Palace stand under a clear sky, every window and flagpole crisp, with tiny figures strolling across the paving.

A souvenir had to look true, so Canaletto drew buildings with great precision, using careful sketches made on the spot. But a picture also has to be a good composition, so he moved buildings, widened squares and combined viewpoints when it helped. Buyers wanted the feeling of Venice more than a survey of it.

People think Canaletto's views are exact snapshots. He often adjusted buildings and viewpoints to fit the picture, combining views from more than one spot or widening a square. He may also have used a camera obscura for some sketches, though how much is debated. Compare a veduta with a map or a photograph and you will find changes.

blocks.title: Snapshot or composition?
blocks.q: In a Canaletto, you can see two buildings side by side that cannot both be seen from any single spot in Venice. What does that show?
steps: A camera, or one eye, sees from one place.
If no single place shows both, the painter combined views.
Canaletto composed the view for the picture.
blocks.a: He adjusted the view: it is a composed picture, not a snapshot.

sources.name: National Gallery of Art: Chardin, Soap Bubbles (1942.9.8); Canaletto, The Square of Saint Mark's, Venice (1983.1.1)

blocks.html: In Britain, the eighteenth century was the age of the portrait. Painters built on the elegance of Van Dyck, who had worked for Charles I a century before. The Grand Manner portrait posed sitters with dignity, in rich fabrics, often full length, against grand landscapes or columns, borrowing poses from ancient statues and Old Master paintings.

The leading theorist was Sir Joshua Reynolds (1723 to 1792), the first president of the Royal Academy of Arts, founded in London in 1768. In his lectures, the Discourses on Art (1769 to 1790), he urged painters to idealize nature, following the Old Masters, and he ranked history painting highest.

Grand Manner portraits by Thomas Gainsborough (The Blue Boy, about 1770) and Joshua Reynolds posed sitters with dignity, rich fabric and landscape backgrounds. Academies ranked portraits below history painting, but portraits paid most artists' bills.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Thomas Gainsborough, The Blue Boy, about 1770. The Huntington Library, Art Museum, and Botanical Gardens, San Marino, California.

blocks.html: Describe. A boy stands full length in a shimmering blue satin suit with lace collar, holding a plumed hat, against a stormy brown landscape. Analyze. The cool blue is the brightest thing on the canvas, set against warm browns; Gainsborough's quick, feathery strokes make the satin flicker. The low viewpoint and the long figure give the boy a grand presence. Interpret. The suit is not the fashion of 1770: it imitates the clothes in Van Dyck's portraits of the 1630s, an homage to the painter Gainsborough admired. A popular story says the blue answered Reynolds's advice to keep blue to small accents, but Reynolds gave that lecture in 1778, about eight years after the painting, so the story is doubtful. The sitter was long said to be Jonathan Buttall, the son of a merchant, but that identification has been debated.

Genre

blocks.cap: The hierarchy of genres taught by the French and British academies.

blocks.html: The ranking was the academies' theory; the market was different. History paintings were large, slow and hard to sell. Wealthy families wanted portraits of themselves for their houses. So most British painters, including Reynolds himself, earned their living from portraits, while dreaming of history painting.

People think the portrait was a minor genre. The academies ranked it below history painting, but portraits were the most common commissions, paid most artists' bills, and include some of the greatest works of the age. Rank in theory is not the same as importance in practice.

blocks.title: Which genre?
blocks.q: A huge canvas shows a Roman general refusing a crown, with twenty figures in togas. Where would an academy rank it, and why?
steps: The subject is a story from history with a moral.
It needs many figures, knowledge of the past and imagination.
That is history painting, the top of the hierarchy.
blocks.a: History painting, the highest rank.

blocks.html: The Blue Boy was sold to the American collector Henry E. Huntington in 1921 for a record price, and its departure from Britain caused an outcry. It has hung in California ever since.

blocks.html: In 1738 excavators began digging at Herculaneum, and in 1748 at Pompeii, the Roman towns buried by Mount Vesuvius in AD 79. Wall paintings, furniture and whole streets came to light. At the same time, the German scholar Johann Joachim Winckelmann praised Greek art for its "noble simplicity and quiet grandeur" (1755). A new taste for the ancient world, more exact than the Renaissance's (see Roman Arches, Concrete and Domes), took hold across Europe and America: Neoclassicism (about 1760 to 1830).

Neoclassical painters rejected the Rococo's pastels and playful curves as frivolous. They wanted clear outlines, calm, balanced compositions, sober color, and stories of Roman virtue: duty, sacrifice and patriotism.

Neoclassicism (about 1760 to 1830) revived Greek and Roman art with clear line, calm color and balanced composition, often carrying a moral message, as in Jacques-Louis David's Oath of the Horatii (1784).

blocks.text: Looking closely: The Oath of the Horatii

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Jacques-Louis David, The Oath of the Horatii, 1784. Louvre, Paris.

blocks.html: Describe. In a plain Roman hall, three brothers stretch out their arms to swear an oath on three swords their father holds up. At the right, the women of the family slump in grief. The story, from the Roman historian Livy, tells of three brothers chosen to fight for Rome. Analyze. Three arches behind divide the scene into three groups: brothers, father, women. The men are drawn with hard, straight lines and stiff, tense poses; the women's curved, drooping forms answer them. The light is clear, the colors few, the space shallow, like a stage or a relief carving. Interpret. Duty to the state outweighs family feeling. David painted it in Rome, signed it in 1784, and showed it at the Paris Salon of 1785, where it was a sensation.

blocks.name: ar-compare
blocks.cap: Neoclassical (A) against Rococo (B): hard line and duty against soft pastel and grace.

blocks.html: The style matched its message. A cause that demands self-control and sacrifice is best shown in a style of order and restraint: straight lines, firm outlines, no frills. In the years around the American and French Revolutions, this Roman idea of civic virtue spoke strongly to many viewers.

People mix up Neoclassical and Renaissance art because both revive antiquity. Neoclassicism (about 1760 to 1830) is cooler and sharper, often frieze-like, with archaeological detail from Pompeii and a moral message. Check the date and the clues: crisp outlines, sober color, a stage-like space and a story of virtue.

blocks.title: Neoclassical or Renaissance?
blocks.q: A painting of about 1790 shows Roman figures in a shallow space, sharply outlined, in sober colors, choosing duty over love. Which style?
steps: The date, about 1790, falls in the Neoclassical period.
Sharp outlines, sober color and a shallow, stage-like space are Neoclassical clues.
A moral of duty over feeling fits the movement.
blocks.a: Neoclassical.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Jacques-Louis David, Napoleon Crossing the Alps, 1801. Château de Malmaison (one of five versions).

blocks.html: David later served Napoleon. In Napoleon Crossing the Alps (1801) the young general rides a rearing horse with a billowing cloak, and the rocks bear the names of Hannibal and Charlemagne, earlier conquerors who crossed the Alps. In fact he crossed on a mule, in fair weather. David painted the heroic image his patron wanted.

blocks.html: In the British colonies of North America there were no academies, few collectors and almost no old paintings to study. Portraits were what people wanted, and a few gifted painters, mostly self-taught, learned from prints and the occasional imported picture. They drew on the British portrait tradition and, after independence, on Neoclassicism.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: John Singleton Copley, Paul Revere, 1768. Museum of Fine Arts, Boston.

blocks.html: Describe. A man in shirt sleeves and an open waistcoat sits at a polished wooden table, chin in hand, holding a silver teapot. Engraving tools lie on the table. Analyze. Strong light from the left falls on his face, white shirt and the teapot against a dark background. The table's reflections and the shine of the silver show off Copley's skill with surfaces. Interpret. Paul Revere (1734 to 1818) was a Boston silversmith and engraver. Copley painted him as a craftsman at work, in working clothes, proud of a skilled trade, which was unusual: wealthy sitters usually wanted silk and columns. Revere later became famous for his midnight ride of 1775, but this portrait, painted seven years earlier, is about his craft.

John Singleton Copley painted Paul Revere (1768) at his workbench as a silversmith; Gilbert Stuart painted George Washington (1796); Thomas Jefferson designed Monticello on Roman and Palladian models.

People think Revere's portrait shows a rider. Copley painted him as a silversmith, holding a teapot he may have made, with engraving tools on the table, in 1768, years before the famous ride. Look at what the sitter holds and wears: they tell you how he wanted to be seen.

John Singleton Copley (1738 to 1815) taught himself in Boston from prints and became the best portraitist in the colonies. In 1774 he left for London and never returned. Gilbert Stuart (1755 to 1828) trained in London and came home to paint the leaders of the new nation. His unfinished Athenaeum Portrait of George Washington (1796), only the head painted, became the model for dozens of copies he sold and, later, for the face on the one-dollar bill.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Gilbert Stuart, George Washington (the Athenaeum Portrait), 1796. Owned jointly by the National Portrait Gallery, Washington, and the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Thomas Jefferson, Monticello, Charlottesville, Virginia, built 1769 to 1809.

blocks.html: Thomas Jefferson designed his own house on a hilltop in Virginia and rebuilt it over forty years, from 1769 to 1809. He based it on the books of the Italian architect Andrea Palladio and on Roman temples: a portico of columns with a triangular pediment, and a shallow dome, which he added after seeing new buildings in Paris, such as the Hôtel de Salm, while he was American minister to France (1784 to 1789). Monticello was the center of a plantation worked by enslaved people, and today the site presents their lives and work alongside the house.

blocks.name: ar-arch
blocks.cap: The classical orders. Monticello's porticoes use columns and a pediment from this tradition.

blocks.html: A young republic looked to the ancient republics for its image. Jefferson wanted American public buildings to follow Roman models, and he used them for the Virginia State Capitol and the University of Virginia as well as his house. The classical style signaled order, learning and citizenship.

blocks.title: Reading a portrait
blocks.q: In Copley's portrait, Revere holds a teapot and has engraving tools before him. What do these choices suggest?
steps: Revere was a silversmith and engraver.
The teapot and tools are the products and instruments of his trade.
Copley shows him as a skilled craftsman, proud of his work.
blocks.a: He is presented as a working silversmith.

blocks.html: Neoclassicism prized reason, order and Roman virtue. Around 1800 many artists, poets and composers turned the other way. Romanticism (about 1790 to 1850) valued feeling over reason, the individual over the rules, imagination over imitation, and above all the power of nature.

A key idea was the sublime. In 1757 the writer Edmund Burke separated the beautiful (small, smooth, pleasing) from the sublime: things so vast or powerful that they fill us with awe, even a thrill of fear, such as mountains, storms, the open sea and the night sky. Romantic painters set out to make viewers feel the sublime.

Romantic artists (about 1800 to 1850) valued strong feeling, awe at nature (the sublime) and the individual: Caspar David Friedrich's Wanderer above the Sea of Fog and J. M. W. Turner's storms and sunsets.

blocks.text: Looking closely: Wanderer above the Sea of Fog

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Caspar David Friedrich, Wanderer above the Sea of Fog, about 1817. Hamburger Kunsthalle, Hamburg.

blocks.html: Describe. A man in a dark green coat, cane in hand, stands on a rocky summit with his back to us, looking out over a sea of fog from which rocky peaks rise. Analyze. The figure is placed right in the center, dark against the pale mist, and the lines of the slopes lead to him. Because we see him from behind (a Rückenfigur, German for "back figure," Friedrich's favorite device), we look with him rather than at him. The far distance dissolves into soft blue-gray haze. Interpret. It is a picture of one person facing the immensity of nature, and of the inner life of the person looking. What he feels, awe, loneliness or mastery, is left to us.

Why the turn to feeling? The French Revolution and the Napoleonic wars shook faith in reason and order, and the new factory cities of the Industrial Revolution made untouched nature seem precious. Romantic artists looked inward, to emotion and imagination, and outward, to wild landscape, as sources of truth.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: J. M. W. Turner, The Fighting Temeraire, 1839. National Gallery, London.

blocks.html: J. M. W. Turner (1775 to 1851) painted light and weather themselves. In The Fighting Temeraire, a pale, ghostly old warship that fought at Trafalgar in 1805 is towed up the Thames by a small, dark steam tug to be broken up, in 1838. Behind them the sun sets in a blaze of orange and gold. The old sailing age gives way to the age of steam, and Turner lets color carry the feeling.

People think "romantic" means "about love." Romanticism is about strong feeling of every kind, awe at nature (the sublime) and the power of imagination. A stormy sea or a lonely mountain top is far more typical of it than a love scene.

blocks.title: Romantic or Neoclassical?
blocks.q: A painting of about 1830 shows a tiny ship in a vast storm, painted with loose, swirling color. Which movement fits, and why?
steps: The subject is nature's overwhelming power: the sublime.
Loose, expressive color carries feeling, not crisp outline.
The tiny human element against nature's scale is typical of Romanticism.
blocks.a: Romanticism.

blocks.name: ar-compare
blocks.cap: Romantic (A) against Neoclassical (B): one person before nature, against a public lesson in duty.

blocks.html: Two painters born in the mid-1700s show how wide the Romantic age was. John Constable (1776 to 1837) spent his life painting a few square miles of the English countryside. Francisco de Goya (1746 to 1828) painted the Spanish court and, later, the darkest sides of human nature.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: John Constable, The Hay Wain, 1821. National Gallery, London.

blocks.html: Describe. A horse-drawn hay cart (a wain) stands in a shallow river beside a cottage, under a huge, changing sky. A dog watches from the bank; meadows stretch away in sunlight. Analyze. Constable broke the greens into many tones and added flecks of white, later called "Constable's snow," to make the leaves and water sparkle. The clouds are studied from life: he made dozens of sky studies outdoors. Interpret. It is a portrait of the Stour valley in Suffolk where he grew up, close to his father's mill, painted with affection and close observation rather than ideal rules.
John Constable painted the English countryside from close outdoor study (The Hay Wain, 1821); Francisco de Goya, court painter in Spain, painted his sitters with sharp honesty.

Constable painted oil sketches outdoors, quickly, to catch the light and weather, then worked up large finished canvases in the studio. The fresh color and broken touch of those sketches entered his big pictures. When The Hay Wain was shown at the Paris Salon in 1824 and won a gold medal from King Charles X, French painters were struck by its freshness.

People think landscape painting was always respected. Academies ranked it low, below history painting and portraits (see the hierarchy of genres). Painters like Constable and Turner, with their large, ambitious canvases, helped raise it. Constable had trouble selling his landscapes in England for years; The Hay Wain sold to a French dealer.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Francisco de Goya, Manuel Osorio Manrique de Zuñiga, about 1787 to 1788. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York.

blocks.html: Goya became painter to the Spanish king in 1786 and First Court Painter in 1799. In this portrait a small boy in a bright red suit holds a pet magpie on a string; a cage of finches sits beside him, and three cats stare hungrily from the shadows. The red suit glows against a plain gray-green ground. The boy is sweet and serious; the watching cats bring a hint of danger into a child's world, and some see in them a reminder of how fragile childhood was. Goya painted the royal family, too, without flattery. Later, after war and illness, he made prints and paintings about war and human folly that are among the darkest in art.

blocks.title: Why the cats?
blocks.q: In Goya's portrait of Manuel Osorio, three cats stare at the boy's pet bird. Give one reading of this detail.
steps: The bird is tied on a string and cannot escape.
The cats, half in shadow, are watching it.
The detail adds tension: innocence watched by danger.
Some scholars connect it to the fragility of childhood; the painting does not say for certain.
blocks.a: The cats add a hint of danger to an innocent scene; its exact meaning is open.

blocks.html: In the 1820s Thomas Cole (1801 to 1848), born in England, began painting the wild Catskill Mountains along the Hudson River in New York. Other painters followed him for half a century. The group never had a formal school; the name Hudson River School was coined in the 1870s, at first dismissively. They brought the Romantic sublime to the American landscape.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Thomas Cole, View from Mount Holyoke, Northampton, Massachusetts, after a Thunderstorm (The Oxbow), 1836. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York.

blocks.html: Describe. From a mountain top we look down on a great loop (an oxbow) of the Connecticut River. On the left are storm clouds, a shattered tree and dark wild forest; on the right, sunlit fields, farms and smoke from chimneys. In the foreground, if you look hard, Cole painted himself at his easel. Analyze. A diagonal divides the canvas: dark and stormy at the left, light and calm at the right. The river's curve leads the eye across the valley. Interpret. The painting sets wilderness beside cultivated land just as the storm passes. Viewers have read it as a celebration of settlement, as a warning about what is lost, or as both; Cole wrote elsewhere of his worry about the cutting of American forests.
Thomas Cole, Frederic Church and Albert Bierstadt painted the American wilderness on a grand scale; Cole's The Oxbow (1836) sets wild hills beside farmland.

A young nation without ancient cathedrals or ruins looked to its land for a sense of greatness. Huge, detailed landscapes of mountains, waterfalls and the West gave Americans an image of their country as vast and new. Frederic Church (1826 to 1900) painted Niagara Falls (1857) and the Andes; Albert Bierstadt (1830 to 1902) painted the Rocky Mountains and Yosemite on canvases many feet wide, which drew paying crowds.

People think these painters copied one view exactly. They sketched outdoors, often in pencil and oil on many trips, then combined sketches from many places into ideal scenes in the studio, adjusting mountains, light and trees. Even The Oxbow, a real view, is arranged for its contrast of storm and sun.

blocks.title: Observed or composed?
blocks.q: A Bierstadt painting shows a mountain range, a waterfall and a lake together. His sketchbooks show each one drawn at a different place. What does that tell us?
steps: The parts were sketched on the spot, from life.
They come from different places.
Bierstadt combined them into one ideal scene.
blocks.a: It is composed in the studio from separate observed sketches.

blocks.cap: A diagonal divides storm from sunlight in The Oxbow.

blocks.html: Around 1850 a group of French painters rejected both the ideal heroes of Neoclassicism and the passionate imagination of Romanticism. They wanted to paint the world as it was, especially the lives of ordinary working people. Gustave Courbet (1819 to 1877) said he could not paint an angel because he had never seen one. The movement is called Realism (about 1840 to 1880).

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Jean-François Millet, The Gleaners, 1857. Musée d'Orsay, Paris.

blocks.html: Describe. Three peasant women bend in a stubble field, picking up stray stalks of wheat left after the harvest. Far behind them, in golden light, are huge haystacks, a loaded cart and many harvesters, with a foreman on horseback. Analyze. The three women fill the foreground, big and heavy, their backs bent in a slow rhythm, their faces hidden. The bright, rich harvest is pushed far away. Interpret. Gleaning, gathering what the harvest leaves behind, was allowed for the poorest families. Millet (1814 to 1875) gave these women the size and dignity usually kept for heroes. Some critics in 1857 found that alarming; others saw it as simple truth about rural life.
Realists painted ordinary people and work without idealizing them: Courbet's The Stone Breakers (1849), Millet's The Gleaners (1857) and Rosa Bonheur's The Horse Fair (1852 to 1855).

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Gustave Courbet, The Stone Breakers, 1849. Destroyed in 1945; known from photographs.

blocks.html: Courbet's The Stone Breakers showed two road workers, an old man and a boy, life-size, breaking stones in torn clothes. Paintings that large were supposed to show history or myth; Courbet used that scale for anonymous laborers. The canvas was destroyed near the end of World War II in 1945, and we know it from photographs.

Why the change? The revolutions of 1848 put working people at the center of public life, and new science praised observation over imagination. For the Realists, choosing an everyday subject was itself a statement: ordinary lives are worth the size and seriousness of a history painting.

People use "realism" to mean any lifelike picture. A Vermeer or a Van Eyck is lifelike but is not part of the movement. The 19th-century Realist movement was about choosing everyday, unheroic subjects, such as laborers, peasants and village funerals, and painting them without idealizing.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Rosa Bonheur, The Horse Fair, 1852 to 1855. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York.

blocks.html: Rosa Bonheur (1822 to 1899), the most famous animal painter of her day, studied the Paris horse market twice a week for a year and a half to paint The Horse Fair. To work freely in that crowded, all-male setting she obtained official police permission to wear trousers. The huge canvas, more than 16 feet wide, swirls with rearing horses and grooms.

blocks.title: Realist or not?
blocks.q: A very lifelike painting of 1850 shows a Greek goddess on a cloud. Is it Realist?
steps: It is lifelike in technique.
But the subject is ideal and imaginary, not everyday life.
The Realist movement is defined by everyday subjects shown without idealizing.
blocks.a: No: lifelike, but not Realist in subject.

blocks.html: For centuries artists had used the camera obscura, a dark box in which a lens throws an image onto a surface (see Vermeer and Canaletto). The problem was to make that image stay. In the 1820s and 1830s several inventors solved it in different ways.

In France, Louis Daguerre presented his process to the Academy of Sciences on January 7, 1839, and the French government made the details public on August 19, 1839. A daguerreotype is a single, mirror-like image on a silver-coated copper plate; it cannot be copied. In England, William Henry Fox Talbot developed a paper negative from which many positive prints could be made; his improved version, the calotype, was patented in 1841. Talbot's negative-positive idea is the basis of film photography.
Daguerre announced the daguerreotype in 1839; by the 1860s photographers such as Julia Margaret Cameron were making photographs as art.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Louis Daguerre, Boulevard du Temple, Paris, 1838. Daguerreotype (destroyed; known from a copy).

blocks.html: Describe. From a high window we look down a long, tree-lined Paris boulevard. The street seems empty, except at the lower left, where a man stands with one foot raised while his boots are polished. Analyze. The exposure took several minutes. Carriages and walkers moved too fast to register and vanished; the man stood still long enough to appear. Interpret. It is often called the first photograph to show a person, by accident. The busy boulevard looks deserted because of the technology, not because it was empty.

People think early photos needed only a click. Early exposures took minutes. Anything that moved blurred or vanished, which is why early street views look empty and why portrait sitters used hidden head braces to hold still. By the 1850s new processes cut exposures to seconds.

Photography changed painting. It could record a likeness faster and cheaper than a portrait painter, so painters asked what painting could do that a camera could not: color, invention, the feeling of light and touch. Photography also froze motion: in 1878 Eadweard Muybridge's photographs of a galloping horse showed all four hooves off the ground at once, something no painter had seen clearly.

blocks.text: Photography as art: Julia Margaret Cameron

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Julia Margaret Cameron, Mrs. Herbert Duckworth, 1867. Albumen silver print. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York.

blocks.html: Julia Margaret Cameron (1815 to 1879) was given a camera in 1863 and took up photography at 48. She made large, close portraits of friends and family with soft focus and strong light from one side, here her niece Julia Jackson in profile. Critics complained about the blur; Cameron chose it, to make portraits that felt like paintings rather than records.

blocks.title: Why is the street empty?
blocks.q: A daguerreotype of 1838 shows a famous busy street with no traffic. Why?
steps: The exposure lasted several minutes.
Moving carriages and people did not stay in one place long enough to register.
Only things that stood still, buildings, trees and one man having his boots shined, appear.
blocks.a: The long exposure erased everything that moved.

blocks.html: After the Civil War (1861 to 1865), American painters trained in greater numbers in Paris and Munich, then came home, or stayed abroad, and painted in their own ways. Building on Realism and on the earlier American portrait, they made an American art that held its own.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Winslow Homer, Breezing Up (A Fair Wind), 1873 to 1876. National Gallery of Art, Washington.

blocks.html: Winslow Homer (1836 to 1910) began as an illustrator, drawing the Civil War for Harper's Weekly, and taught himself to paint. In Breezing Up a small catboat heels over in a stiff wind off Gloucester, Massachusetts, with three boys and a fisherman aboard. The boat makes a strong diagonal against the choppy green sea; the sail is cut off by the frame, so we feel the speed. Later Homer lived on the Maine coast and painted the sea's power.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Henry Ossawa Tanner, The Banjo Lesson, 1893. Hampton University Museum, Hampton, Virginia.

blocks.html: Describe. In a plain room, an older man sits with a boy on his knee, helping him play a banjo that is almost too big for him. A table with dishes and a pot stand nearby. Analyze. Two kinds of light meet in the picture: a cool, bluish daylight from the left and the warm glow of a fire at the right. The heads bend together over the instrument, and the light gathers on the hands, the strings and the boy's face. Interpret. It is a scene of patience and love passed from one generation to the next. Henry Ossawa Tanner (1859 to 1937), the leading African American painter of his time, studied with Thomas Eakins in Philadelphia and moved to Paris in 1891. He painted this on a visit home, choosing to show the people of his community with dignity at a time when popular images often mocked them.
Winslow Homer painted the sea and country life, John Singer Sargent dazzling portraits, and Henry Ossawa Tanner The Banjo Lesson (1893): American subjects in their own distinct ways.

People think American art only copied Europe. Homer, Thomas Eakins and Tanner trained partly abroad but painted distinctly American subjects: New England fishermen, rowers on Philadelphia's river, family life in the American South. Training abroad is not the same as copying.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: John Singer Sargent, The Daughters of Edward Darley Boit, 1882. Museum of Fine Arts, Boston.

blocks.html: John Singer Sargent (1856 to 1925), born in Florence to American parents, painted the four daughters of a Boston family in their Paris apartment. Instead of a neat row, he scattered them through a deep, dark space, beside two enormous Japanese vases, like a modern Las Meninas. James McNeill Whistler (1834 to 1903) went further from storytelling: he titled the portrait of his mother Arrangement in Grey and Black No. 1 (1871), insisting it was mainly an arrangement of color and shape.

Why train in Europe? America had few art schools and museums until late in the century. Paris offered drawing from life, great collections and the Salon. But the artists chose their own subjects, and some, like Homer, spent most of their careers painting American life.

blocks.title: Reading the light
blocks.q: In The Banjo Lesson, where do the two lights come from, and what do they do?
steps: A cool daylight enters from the left.
A warm firelight glows at the right.
They meet on the figures and the banjo, drawing the eye to the lesson.
blocks.a: Daylight and firelight meet on the man, the boy and the banjo.
