blocks.html: During the Edo period (1603 to 1868), Japan was ruled by the Tokugawa shoguns from Edo, today's Tokyo, and was largely closed to the outside world. Its cities grew rich, and townspeople spent money on theater, fashion, travel and pictures. The pictures they bought most were ukiyo-e, "pictures of the floating world," the world of fleeting pleasures: kabuki actors, celebrated beauties, festivals and, later, famous landscapes. You met earlier Japanese painting and European woodcuts in Art History I.

A ukiyo-e print was a team effort. A publisher chose the subject and paid for everything. A designer, such as Hokusai or Hiroshige, drew the picture in ink on thin paper. A carver pasted the drawing onto a block of cherry wood and cut away everything but the lines. More blocks were cut, one for each color. A printer brushed water-based color on each block in turn and pressed the paper onto it by hand with a flat pad, lining it up with notches cut in the blocks so the colors fit.
Edo-period prints of the "floating world" were made by a team: a publisher, a designer such as Hokusai or Hiroshige, a carver and a printer, with one block for each color.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Katsushika Hokusai, Under the Wave off Kanagawa (The Great Wave), about 1830 to 1832. Woodblock print. Many impressions, for example The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

blocks.html: Describe. A huge wave curls over three long boats full of rowers; its foam breaks into claw-like fingers. Far behind, small and still, is Mount Fuji. Analyze. The wave fills the left side and arcs over the boats; the low, distant Fuji sits in the hollow it makes, so the eye goes from the wave's crest down to the mountain. The deep blue is Prussian blue, a strong, lasting synthetic pigment newly imported from Europe. A low viewpoint and Western-style depth (the mountain made small by distance) were new in Japanese prints. Interpret. Nature's force against human effort, and the calm, sacred mountain within the storm. It is the first print in Hokusai's series Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji (1830 to 1832).

People think Hokusai carved and printed The Great Wave himself. He designed it; professional carvers cut the blocks and printers made the prints, for a publisher. That is also why thousands of impressions existed and many survive in museums around the world: each is an original print from the same blocks.

The team system and the cheap materials kept prices low, about the price of a bowl of noodles for an ordinary print. Large editions meant townspeople, not only nobles, could own art. Landscapes boomed in the 1830s as travel within Japan grew, and series such as Hiroshige's One Hundred Famous Views of Edo (1856 to 1858) sold like postcards.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Utagawa Hiroshige, Sudden Shower over Shin-Ōhashi Bridge and Atake, 1857. From One Hundred Famous Views of Edo.

blocks.html: In Hiroshige's print, people hurry across a wooden bridge under a sudden summer rain, drawn as fine, dark lines over the whole sheet. The bridge cuts diagonally across the picture, seen from above. Each rain line had to be carved by hand.

blocks.title: Who did what?
blocks.q: A museum label reads: "Designed by Katsushika Hokusai, published by Nishimuraya Yohachi." Who carved and printed it?
steps: The label names the designer and the publisher.
Carvers and printers were skilled craftsmen who were usually not named.
So the carving and printing were done by unnamed members of the team, not by Hokusai.
blocks.a: Unnamed professional carvers and printers working for the publisher.

blocks.html: Japan's great families, the military lords (daimyō), the shoguns and rich merchants, decorated their castles and houses with folding screens (byōbu) and painted sliding doors. A screen is usually six panels joined by hinges, often made as a pair. Many were painted on gold leaf, which glowed in dim rooms lit by lamps and by light reflected from paper windows. Like the ukiyo-e prints of the towns, screens belong to Japan's early modern age, but they were made for the elite.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Ogata Kōrin, Irises, about 1701 to 1705. Ink and color on gold leaf, pair of six-panel folding screens. Nezu Museum, Tokyo.

blocks.html: Describe. Clumps of blue-violet irises with green leaves march across a plain gold ground, with no water, no sky and no horizon. Analyze. Kōrin (1658 to 1716) used only a few colors: mineral azurite blue and malachite green on gold. The clumps repeat, some almost exactly, in a rhythm that rises and falls across the panels. With no ground line, the gold reads as both space and flat surface. Interpret. Educated viewers knew a famous episode from The Tales of Ise, a Heian-period poem tale, set at a place called Yatsuhashi ("Eight Bridges") where irises bloomed. Kōrin left out the bridges and the travelers and kept only the flowers, trusting viewers to remember the story. The work belongs to the Rinpa school of bold, decorative design.
Folding screens on gold leaf, such as Ogata Kōrin's Irises (about 1705), and castles like Himeji (completed 1609) show the splendor of Japan's great families.

People read a folding screen as a flat painting. It stands in a zigzag, so the picture folds in and out, and the gold catches the light differently on each panel. Kōrin's irises seem to step forward and back as the panels turn. Imagine it standing in a room, not hanging flat on a wall.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Hasegawa Tōhaku, Pine Trees, late 1500s. Ink on paper, pair of six-panel folding screens. Tokyo National Museum.

blocks.html: Not all screens were gold. Hasegawa Tōhaku (1539 to 1610) painted Pine Trees in ink alone, in the Momoyama period just before Edo began. Pines loom out of mist and fade into it; large parts of the paper are left blank, so the empty space becomes fog. It is a National Treasure of Japan. Whether Tōhaku meant it as a finished work or as a study is debated.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Himeji Castle, Himeji, Japan, main keep completed 1609.

blocks.html: Castles were built in a burst of construction around 1600, as warlords fought to unify Japan. Himeji, largely completed between 1601 and 1609 under the lord Ikeda Terumasa, rises on stone walls with layered white plaster roofs, which earned it the name "White Heron Castle." It survived wars, fires and earthquakes and is a World Heritage Site. Its rooms were the setting for painted screens and doors.

Gold and big, bold motifs were practical as well as splendid. In castle halls lit by small windows and oil lamps, gold reflects light into the room, and large, simple shapes read well from across the space. The zigzag stand also keeps a screen upright without any frame.

blocks.title: Why no bridge?
blocks.q: Kōrin's Irises illustrates a scene from The Tales of Ise at the Eight Bridges. Why might he show only the irises?
steps: Educated viewers knew the story well.
The flowers alone were enough to call it to mind.
Leaving out the bridges and people makes a bolder, more decorative design.
blocks.a: The irises suggest the whole story to viewers who knew it, and make a stronger design.

blocks.html: Two dynasties ruled China in this period: the Ming (1368 to 1644), founded after Mongol rule ended, and the Qing (1644 to 1912), founded by the Manchus from the northeast. Both built on the arts you met in Bronzes, Clay Soldiers and Porcelain and Chinese Landscape Painting.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: The Hall of Supreme Harmony, Forbidden City, Beijing. Palace built 1406 to 1420; this hall rebuilt 1695 to 1697.

blocks.html: The Ming Yongle emperor moved the capital to Beijing and built a vast walled palace there from 1406 to 1420. It was called the Forbidden City because ordinary people could not enter. Its halls stand on a north-south axis, one behind another, on white marble terraces, with yellow-glazed roof tiles, a color reserved for the emperor. The Hall of Supreme Harmony, the largest, where the emperor held great ceremonies, was rebuilt under the Qing in 1695 to 1697 after a fire. Wooden buildings like these were often rebuilt, keeping the old plan and forms. It is now the Palace Museum.

blocks.text: Looking closely: a Ming blue-and-white jar

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Blue-and-White Jar with a Dragon, Ming dynasty, early 1400s. Jingdezhen kilns. Porcelain with cobalt blue under clear glaze. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York.

blocks.html: Describe. A round porcelain jar is painted with a long, scaly dragon chasing through clouds, with bands of waves and petals at the neck and foot. Analyze. The blue was painted in cobalt on the raw white clay, then covered with a clear glaze and fired at very high heat, so the color lies under the glassy surface and cannot wear off. The dragon twists around the curve of the jar, so you must turn it, or walk around it, to follow its body. Interpret. The dragon was an imperial emblem. Blue-and-white porcelain from the kilns of Jingdezhen went to the court and was traded across Asia, to the Islamic world and later to Europe in huge quantities.

The Ming (1368 to 1644) built the Forbidden City in Beijing (1406 to 1420) and made fine blue-and-white porcelain; literati scholar-painters valued personal brushwork over likeness. The Qing ruled after them, from 1644 to 1912.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Shen Zhou, Poet on a Mountaintop, about 1500. Ink and light color on paper, album leaf mounted as a handscroll. Nelson-Atkins Museum of Art, Kansas City.

blocks.html: Scholar-officials, the literati, painted as an expression of learning and character rather than as a trade. Shen Zhou (1427 to 1509), who never took office and lived near Suzhou, founded what is called the Wu school. In Poet on a Mountaintop, a small figure stands on a cliff above misty valleys; a poem written in Shen Zhou's hand fills the upper left. For the literati, poetry, calligraphy and painting were one art, and the brushstroke showed the person.

Literati painting valued what the brush revealed about the painter: learning, calm and character. Copying nature exactly was the work of professional court painters. That is why literati paintings often use ink and light color, refer to older masters and include poems.

People think "Ming vase" means any old Chinese vase. The Ming dynasty ruled from 1368 to 1644; the Qing came after, from 1644 to 1912, and made porcelain too, as did earlier dynasties. A museum dates a vase by its reign marks, shape, decoration, glaze and clay.

blocks.title: Ming or Qing?
blocks.q: A porcelain bowl carries a reign mark of the Kangxi emperor, who ruled from 1661 to 1722. Is it a Ming bowl?
steps: Kangxi ruled from 1661 to 1722.
The Ming dynasty ended in 1644.
So a genuine Kangxi mark points to the Qing dynasty.
blocks.a: No: it is Qing.

blocks.name: ar-timeline
blocks.cap: The Ming and Qing dynasties, with Song China before them and Joseon Korea and Edo Japan alongside.

blocks.html: The Joseon dynasty ruled Korea from 1392 until 1897, when Korea was proclaimed an empire, which lasted until 1910. Its rulers followed Neo-Confucian ideals of modesty, order and learning, and those ideals shaped its arts. Korea traded with and learned from Ming and Qing China, but its potters and painters developed tastes of their own.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Moon Jar, Joseon dynasty, second half of the 1700s. Porcelain. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York.

blocks.html: Describe. A large, round white porcelain jar with no painted decoration at all. Moon jars are typically about 40 centimeters (16 inches) tall. Analyze. It is not a perfect sphere. Potters threw two large bowls on the wheel and joined them rim to rim, and the seam around the middle and the slight lean of the form remain visible. The glaze is a soft, milky white with faint tints where the kiln's heat varied. Interpret. Its plain, gentle shape and quiet color, like a full moon, suit the Joseon taste for simplicity and naturalness. Its small irregularities are part of its beauty, not mistakes.
Joseon Korea (1392 to 1897) prized plain white porcelain such as the round moon jars, and Jeong Seon painted "true-view" landscapes of real Korean mountains.

Neo-Confucian thought valued restraint and frugality. At court, plain white porcelain was preferred to colorful wares, and white suited Confucian rituals. A jar made by joining two halves also had a practical side: a single piece that large would sag on the wheel.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Jeong Seon, Clearing after Rain on Mount Inwang, 1751. Ink on paper, hanging scroll. Leeum Museum of Art, Seoul.

blocks.html: For centuries Korean painters had painted ideal landscapes in Chinese styles, often of places they had never seen. Jeong Seon (1676 to 1759) painted real Korean places from his own observation, a style called true-view landscape (jingyeong sansu). Clearing after Rain on Mount Inwang (1751) shows the granite peaks of a mountain in Seoul, wet and dark after rain, with bands of white mist below. He used heavy, wet strokes laid side by side for the rock and dots for the pines. Later, Kim Hong-do (born 1745) extended the same interest in real Korean life to lively genre scenes of farmers, schoolchildren and wrestlers.

People think Korean art is a branch of Chinese art. Korea learned from China, as Japan did, but Korean painters and potters built their own styles and tastes: moon jars unlike any Chinese porcelain, true-view paintings of Korean mountains, and genre scenes of Korean daily life.

blocks.title: Mistake or style?
blocks.q: A moon jar leans slightly and shows a seam around its middle. Is it a failed pot?
steps: Moon jars were made by joining two thrown halves, so a seam is expected.
Large wet clay forms sag a little in firing.
Joseon taste valued natural, unforced forms.
blocks.a: No: the seam and gentle lean come from how it was made, and are part of its admired character.

blocks.html: The Mughal emperors, descended from Central Asian conquerors, ruled much of South Asia from 1526 until 1857. They brought Persian traditions of the illustrated book and garden design and joined them with Indian craft traditions (see Temples of South and Southeast Asia). The great patrons were Akbar (ruled 1556 to 1605), Jahangir (1605 to 1627) and Shah Jahan (1628 to 1658).

Akbar set up imperial workshops where Persian and Indian painters worked together on huge illustrated books. Jahangir loved close observation: portraits, birds, animals and flowers. Painters worked in opaque watercolor and gold on paper, with fine brushes, some said to be made of a single hair.

blocks.text: Looking closely: Shah Jahan on Horseback

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Payag, Shah Jahan on Horseback, about 1630. Ink, watercolor and gold on paper. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York.

blocks.html: Describe. The emperor Shah Jahan rides a stallion in profile across a green ground, holding a spear, a golden halo behind his head. A wide border of painted flowers frames the page. Analyze. Horse and rider are drawn in crisp outline and placed against a plain, pale background, so every detail of jewels, harness and textile stands out. The profile view was standard for imperial portraits: it shows a clear, dignified likeness. Interpret. The halo, borrowed from European religious pictures that came to the court, marks the emperor's semi-divine status. The page was made for an album of portraits and calligraphy.
Mughal emperors in India sponsored jewel-like manuscript and album paintings and built the Taj Mahal (1632 to 1653), Shah Jahan's tomb for his wife Mumtaz Mahal.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: The Taj Mahal, Agra, India, 1632 to 1653.

blocks.html: Shah Jahan's wife Mumtaz Mahal died in 1631. The next year he began a tomb for her on the bank of the Yamuna River at Agra. The white marble mausoleum stands on a raised platform with four minarets at its corners, under a great onion-shaped dome. It stands at the end of a four-part garden (charbagh), divided by water channels, an image of paradise in Persian and Islamic tradition. The marble is inlaid with colored stones in floral designs and with verses of the Qur'an in black stone. The chief architect is usually named as Ustad Ahmad Lahauri, though the records are not complete. Shah Jahan himself was later buried beside her.

blocks.name: ar-compare
blocks.cap: Two great domed buildings of the Islamic world: a Mughal tomb (A) and an Ottoman mosque (B).

blocks.html: People think the Taj Mahal is a palace. It is a tomb (a mausoleum), set in a garden, with a mosque and a guest hall on either side. The emperors' palaces were in the Red Forts at Agra and Delhi.

Symmetry carries the meaning. The tomb is perfectly symmetrical on its axis, mirrored in the long water channel, so that the whole complex reads as one ordered image of a heavenly garden. Only Shah Jahan's own tomb, added off-center beside his wife's, breaks that symmetry.

blocks.title: Palace or tomb?
blocks.q: A building stands in a walled garden with water channels, with a mosque on one side and a matching hall on the other, and the burial chambers of an empress below. Palace or tomb?
steps: The burials make it a mausoleum.
The garden recalls paradise, fitting a tomb.
The palace of the emperor was elsewhere, in the Red Fort.
blocks.a: A tomb, like the Taj Mahal.

blocks.html: In the 1500s and 1600s two great Islamic empires stood side by side: the Ottoman Empire, with its capital at Istanbul, and the Safavid Empire of Iran. Both built on the mosque forms and decorative arts you met in Córdoba and the Alhambra and The Mosque and Its Parts, and each developed its own style.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Mimar Sinan, Süleymaniye Mosque, Istanbul, 1550 to 1557.

blocks.html: Describe. On a hill above the Golden Horn, a great central dome rises over a cascade of half domes and smaller domes, with four slender, pencil-shaped minarets at the corners of the courtyard. Analyze. Inside, the dome rests on four huge piers and is buttressed by two half domes, a plan inspired by the Byzantine church of Hagia Sophia, which the Ottomans had made a mosque after taking the city in 1453. Rows of windows in the dome and walls flood the space with light. The mosque stands at the center of a complex with schools, a hospital, a kitchen for the poor and baths. Interpret. Built for Sultan Süleyman I, it showed the empire's power and its care for its people. Its architect, Mimar Sinan (about 1490 to 1588), served as chief imperial architect for about fifty years.
The architect Sinan built the Süleymaniye Mosque in Istanbul (1550 to 1557), with Iznik tiles inside; in Isfahan the Safavid Shah Mosque (1611 to about 1630) glows with blue tile.

People think Ottoman mosques copied Hagia Sophia exactly. Sinan learned from it but built lighter domes on clearer supports, with many more windows, and arranged the half domes and buttresses more openly. He called the Süleymaniye the work of his journeyman years and the Selimiye Mosque in Edirne (1568 to 1575) his masterpiece.

Iznik tiles. The town of Iznik made fine quartz-based ceramics and tiles for the Ottoman court, painted in cobalt blue, turquoise and green and, from the 1550s, a bright tomato red raised slightly above the surface. Tulips, carnations and leafy vines covered the walls of mosques and palaces.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Shah Mosque (Imam Mosque), Isfahan, Iran, 1611 to about 1630. Tiled vault of the entrance.

blocks.html: In 1598 Shah Abbas I moved the Safavid capital to Isfahan and laid out a vast new square, Naqsh-e Jahan, with a palace, a bazaar and two mosques around it. The Shah Mosque, at the south end, is covered inside and out in glazed tile, mostly blue. To work fast, its builders used haft rangi ("seven-color") tiles, square tiles each painted with part of a pattern, instead of slow mosaic of cut pieces. In the entrance, muqarnas, honeycomb-like vaulting, breaks the light into hundreds of small facets.

Both empires used architecture as a public statement of faith and rule. A mosque complex served the city: prayer, learning, health and charity in one place. Tile was durable in sun and rain, and it turned walls into gardens of color that the inscriptions and patterns made legible from far away.

blocks.title: Mosaic or haft rangi?
blocks.q: A tiled wall is built of square tiles, each painted with several colors that together form a large flower pattern. Is it cut mosaic?
steps: Cut mosaic uses many small pieces, each of one color.
These are squares painted with several colors.
That is the haft rangi method, faster than mosaic.
blocks.a: No: it is haft rangi (painted square tiles).

blocks.name: ar-arch
blocks.cap: The parts of a mosque: prayer hall, mihrab, minbar, minaret and courtyard.

blocks.html: In the 1860s a group of young painters in Paris, among them Claude Monet, Pierre-Auguste Renoir, Camille Pissarro, Alfred Sisley, Edgar Degas and Berthe Morisot, grew tired of the official Salon, whose juries favored polished history paintings. Like the Realists they painted modern life, but their real subject was light: how it changes from hour to hour and how it breaks into color.

On April 15, 1874, they opened their own exhibition in the former studio of the photographer Nadar on the Boulevard des Capucines. A critic, Louis Leroy, mocked a harbor view by Monet titled Impression, Sunrise and called the whole group "Impressionists." They kept the name. Eight group shows followed until 1886.
The Impressionists painted light and modern life with visible, broken brushstrokes, often outdoors. Their first group show was in Paris in 1874, and Monet's Impression, Sunrise gave them their name.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Claude Monet, Impression, Sunrise, 1872. Musée Marmottan Monet, Paris.

blocks.html: Describe. The harbor of Le Havre at dawn: misty blue-gray water and sky, dim shapes of ships and smokestacks, small dark rowboats, and an orange sun with its reflection streaking across the water. Analyze. The paint is thin and quick; the brushstrokes stay visible as separate dabs and dashes. Edges dissolve in the haze. The orange sun is set against its complement, blue, so it glows, even though its value is nearly the same as the sky's. Interpret. The subject is not the port but a moment of light and atmosphere. Monet's title said so: this is an impression.

New tools made outdoor painting easier. Oil paint sold in squeezable metal tubes (invented in 1841) and portable easels let painters work outside, en plein air, finishing a canvas quickly before the light changed. New bright pigments widened the palette. And painters noticed, as scientists were explaining, that shadows are not gray or brown but full of color, often blue or violet.

People think the Impressionists were sloppy. Their quick, broken strokes were a careful method for catching changing light: colors placed side by side to mix in the eye, painted fast because the light would not wait. Many works were reworked in the studio. Stand back from an Impressionist painting and the strokes turn into water, leaves and air.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Claude Monet, Woman with a Parasol: Madame Monet and Her Son, 1875. National Gallery of Art, Washington.

blocks.html: In Woman with a Parasol Monet painted his wife, Camille, and their son on a breezy hill, seen from below against the sky. Grass, dress and clouds are made of the same quick strokes; her veil and skirt blow in the wind. The shadow side of her dress is blue and lilac, colored by the sky.

blocks.title: Why is the shadow blue?
blocks.q: In Woman with a Parasol, the shaded side of the white dress is painted blue and violet. Is Monet wrong?
steps: Outdoors, a white surface in shadow is lit by the blue sky, not the sun.
So the shadow takes on a cool, bluish color.
Monet painted the color he saw, not the gray he was taught.
blocks.a: No: shadows outdoors are lit by blue skylight, so they look bluish.

blocks.html: If Impressionism is about light, the same subject looks different at every hour. Claude Monet (1840 to 1926) took that idea further than anyone. From 1890 on he painted series: one subject, again and again, under different light and weather.

blocks.text: Looking closely: Stacks of Wheat (End of Summer)

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Claude Monet, Stacks of Wheat (End of Summer), 1890 to 1891. The Art Institute of Chicago.

blocks.html: Describe. Two tall stacks of harvested wheat stand in a field near Monet's home at Giverny, with trees, houses and hills behind. Analyze. The stacks are lit from the side by low sun; their shadows are not brown but blue and violet, and their sunny sides glow orange and pink. The whole canvas is woven of small, thick strokes in many colors. Interpret. The stacks hardly matter in themselves. They are a steady shape on which Monet could record light and air at one particular hour.

Monet painted about twenty-five canvases of the wheatstacks in late 1890 and early 1891, in summer haze, autumn sun, frost and snow. He would work on several canvases in the field at once, switching as the light changed. In 1891 he showed fifteen of them together in Paris, and they sold quickly. Next came poplars, then about thirty views of the front of Rouen Cathedral (1892 to 1894), its stone dissolving in morning blue and afternoon gold.
Monet painted the same subject (grainstacks, Rouen Cathedral, water lilies) again and again to show how light and weather change it.

People think the series are copies of one picture. Each canvas records a different hour, season or weather, with different colors. Monet worked on many at once and moved from one to the next as the light changed, then finished them in the studio so they would hang well together.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Claude Monet, Water Lilies, 1906. The Art Institute of Chicago.

blocks.html: At Giverny, Monet built a water garden with a pond, a Japanese-style footbridge and water lilies. For the last decades of his life he painted it in a series of more than 250 canvases. In this one there is no shore and no sky, only the surface of the water with floating lilies and the reflected clouds and trees. Late in life, despite failing eyesight, he painted huge water-lily panels that wrap around two oval rooms at the Musée de l'Orangerie in Paris.

A series lets you see what changes by holding everything else still. With the same subject in every canvas, the differences in color are the light itself: you compare frosty morning to summer evening as a scientist compares measurements, but the result is painting.

blocks.title: Copies or a series?
blocks.q: Two Monet canvases show the same cathedral front from the same window. One is mostly blue and gray, the other orange and gold. What explains the difference?
steps: The subject and viewpoint are the same.
The colors differ because the light differs: cool morning against warm afternoon sun.
Each canvas records a different time and weather.
blocks.a: Two different moments of light: a series, not copies.

blocks.html: Not all the Impressionists painted landscapes. Paris was being rebuilt with wide boulevards, cafés, theaters, parks and railway stations, and several painters made this modern city life their subject.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Edgar Degas, The Dance Class, 1874. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York.

blocks.html: Describe. In a rehearsal room of the Paris Opéra, young dancers in white tutus stretch, wait, scratch and fix their sashes while one performs for the old ballet master, Jules Perrot, who leans on his stick. Analyze. The floorboards rush back in a steep diagonal; the view is from slightly above, off-center, as if we had just walked in. Figures are cut off at the edge, as in a snapshot or a Japanese print. Interpret. It is not a performance but the work behind it: tiredness, boredom and discipline. Edgar Degas (1834 to 1917) painted it in the studio, from drawings and memory, building the scene with great care.
Edgar Degas painted dancers and racehorses, Pierre-Auguste Renoir crowds at leisure, and Berthe Morisot and Mary Cassatt the lives of women and children.

People think Degas painted outdoors like Monet. He worked mostly in the studio, from drawings, memory and sometimes photographs, and he disliked being called an Impressionist; he preferred to be called a Realist or an "Independent." He still showed in the Impressionist exhibitions and shared their interest in modern life and unusual viewpoints.

Paris itself had changed. Between the 1850s and 1870s Baron Haussmann's rebuilding cut wide new boulevards through the old city, and railways, cafés, theaters and riverside resorts gave people new ways to spend free time. Painters who wanted to be "of their time" found their subjects in these new spaces and in the people who used them.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Pierre-Auguste Renoir, Luncheon of the Boating Party, 1880 to 1881. The Phillips Collection, Washington.

blocks.html: Pierre-Auguste Renoir (1841 to 1919) painted his friends relaxing on the balcony of the Maison Fournaise, a restaurant beside the Seine at Chatou, after a day of boating. Light filters through the striped awning onto straw hats, glasses and fruit. The figures, real people from Renoir's circle, talk, flirt and lean on the railing. It is a picture of modern leisure, warm, crowded and happy.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Berthe Morisot, The Cradle, 1872. Musée d'Orsay, Paris.

blocks.html: Women painters could not go everywhere men could: not into cafés alone at night or backstage at the Opéra. Berthe Morisot (1841 to 1895), a founding member who showed at the first exhibition in 1874, painted the private spaces she knew. In The Cradle her sister Edma watches her sleeping baby through a veil of white muslin; a diagonal links the mother's gaze to the child. The American Mary Cassatt (1844 to 1926), who settled in Paris in 1874 and joined the group at Degas's invitation in 1877, painted women and children with the same frankness. In Little Girl in a Blue Armchair (1878) a bored child sprawls in an overstuffed chair. Degas, Cassatt wrote, helped her with the background.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Mary Cassatt, Little Girl in a Blue Armchair, 1878. National Gallery of Art, Washington.

blocks.title: Studio or outdoors?
blocks.q: A Degas painting shows a horse race with jockeys cut off at the edges and a steep, high viewpoint. Was it painted on the spot, like a Monet landscape?
steps: Degas worked mostly in the studio from drawings and memory.
The cropped, snapshot-like composition was carefully designed.
So it was composed in the studio, not painted outdoors on the spot.
blocks.a: Most likely composed in the studio.

blocks.html: For more than two centuries Japan allowed almost no foreign trade. In 1853 and 1854 the American Commodore Matthew Perry forced it open, and trade treaties followed. Japanese goods, including ukiyo-e prints, fans, ceramics and textiles, poured into Europe and the United States. The Paris world's fair of 1867 showed Japanese arts to huge crowds. In 1872 the French critic Philippe Burty gave the craze its name: Japonisme.

Western artists saw in the prints a new way of making pictures: flat areas of bright color, bold outlines, no shading, high or tilted viewpoints, figures cut off by the edge, empty space as part of the design, and everyday subjects. Whistler, Degas, Cassatt, Van Gogh, Toulouse-Lautrec and many others studied them.
After Japan opened to trade in the 1850s, Japanese prints poured into Europe; their flat color, bold cropping and high viewpoints inspired Degas, Van Gogh, Cassatt and others.

blocks.text: Looking closely: Van Gogh copies Hiroshige

blocks.name: ar-compare
blocks.cap: Hiroshige's print of 1857 (A) and Van Gogh's painted copy of 1887 (B).

blocks.html: Describe. In 1887 in Paris, Vincent van Gogh copied Hiroshige's Sudden Shower over Shin-Ōhashi Bridge and Atake in oil paint. The bridge, the hurrying figures and the slanting rain are all there. Analyze. Van Gogh enlarged the scene, made the colors stronger (a vivid yellow bridge, a green-blue river) and added a wide border filled with Japanese characters copied from other prints, in red and green. The flat color areas and the bridge cutting diagonally across the picture come straight from the print. Interpret. Van Gogh was learning. He and his brother Theo collected hundreds of Japanese prints, and he wrote that all his work was based to some extent on Japanese art. The copy shows him absorbing its flatness, its strong color and its bold design.

Japanese prints offered an alternative to the rules Western artists had followed since the Renaissance: one-point perspective, modeling in light and shade, a centered subject. At a moment when photography was taking over exact description, those rules looked less necessary, and the prints showed that a picture could be strong, flat and decorative instead.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec, Divan Japonais, 1893. Color lithograph poster.

blocks.html: Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec (1864 to 1901) used the same lessons for posters: flat silhouettes, a high viewpoint, figures cut by the edge and bold lettering. Divan Japonais advertised a Paris café-concert decorated in Japanese style.

People think the influence went only one way. In the same years, after the Meiji government took power in 1868, many Japanese artists studied Western oil painting, perspective and shading, and the government invited European teachers. Exchange went in both directions, and Japanese printmakers like Hokusai had already absorbed Western perspective decades earlier.

blocks.title: Spot the Japanese lessons
blocks.q: A Paris painting of 1880 shows a theater box from high above, with a figure cut in half by the frame and a large empty area of flat color. Name the Japanese print lessons.
steps: A high viewpoint looking down.
Bold cropping: a figure cut by the edge.
A flat area of color used as part of the design.
blocks.a: High viewpoint, cropping and flat color.

blocks.html: Georges Seurat (1859 to 1891) admired the Impressionists' bright color but not their quick, intuitive method. He wanted color to be as systematic as science. He read color theorists such as Michel-Eugène Chevreul, who showed that colors placed side by side change each other, and that complementary colors intensify each other when they are next to one another.

Seurat's method, which he called chromoluminarism and others call pointillism or divisionism, was to place small dots or dashes of pure color side by side, unmixed on the palette, so that the viewer's eye would combine them at a distance. Orange dots among green ones make a sunlit lawn; blue dots in the orange make shadow.
Georges Seurat placed small dots of pure color side by side for the eye to blend, as in A Sunday on La Grande Jatte (1884 to 1886).

blocks.text: Looking closely: A Sunday on La Grande Jatte

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Georges Seurat, A Sunday on La Grande Jatte, 1884 to 1886. The Art Institute of Chicago.

blocks.html: Describe. Parisians of every class spend a Sunday afternoon on an island park in the Seine: couples strolling, a woman fishing, a man lying on the grass, children, dogs, a monkey on a leash, boats on the river. Analyze. The canvas is about 2 by 3 meters, covered in tiny touches of color. The figures are stiff and still, most in strict profile or front view, arranged in rows and spaced like columns, with long shadows across the grass. Seurat worked on it for two years from dozens of drawings and oil sketches, and added a painted border of dots later. Interpret. It takes the Impressionist subject of modern leisure and freezes it into something calm and timeless, compared by critics to ancient Egyptian or Greek friezes. It was shown at the eighth and last Impressionist exhibition in 1886.

blocks.name: ar-wheel
blocks.cap: Seurat set complements side by side: orange and blue, red and green, to make each more intense.

blocks.html: Color mixed in the eye is not the same as color mixed in paint. Mixing paints on a palette tends to dull them, because each pigment absorbs more light (see subtractive mixing). Dots of pure color placed side by side stay bright. But the eye does not blend them perfectly into a flat new color; the surface shimmers.

People think the dots blend into smooth color up close. They blend only from a distance, and even then the effect shimmers and vibrates rather than mixing like paint. Walk up to the canvas and the dots separate again. Seurat wanted that luminous vibration.

blocks.title: Near and far
blocks.q: A painting is made of alternating red and yellow dots. What do you see from one step away, and from ten steps away?
steps: Close up, the eye can still separate the dots: red and yellow.
From far away, the dots are too small to separate, so the eye combines them.
The combined color reads as a vibrating orange, brighter than a dull mixed paint.
blocks.a: Separate red and yellow dots up close; a shimmering orange from far away.

blocks.name: ar-compare
blocks.cap: Seurat (A) froze modern leisure into rows and dots; Renoir (B) painted it warm and loose.

blocks.html: Vincent van Gogh (1853 to 1890) was Dutch. He worked as an art dealer, a teacher and a lay preacher before he decided, at 27, to become an artist. He taught himself, first with dark, earthy pictures of peasants in the Netherlands, then in Paris (1886 to 1888), where he met the Impressionists and Seurat and discovered Japanese prints. His colors exploded.

In 1888 he moved to Arles in the south of France, hoping to found a community of artists. He painted sunflowers to decorate the house where he hoped Paul Gauguin would join him; Gauguin came for two months that autumn. In 1889 and 1890 Van Gogh stayed at a hospital in Saint-Rémy, where he went on painting. He died in 1890, at 37. In about ten years he made around 2,100 works, including some 860 oil paintings, most in his last two years. His letters to his brother Theo, who supported him, tell us how he worked.
Van Gogh used thick paint (impasto), swirling strokes and strong color to express feeling, as in The Starry Night (1889) and his Sunflowers (1888).

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Vincent van Gogh, The Starry Night, 1889. Museum of Modern Art, New York.

blocks.html: Describe. Above a sleeping village with a church spire, a night sky churns with swirling currents, a glowing crescent moon and stars ringed with halos of light. A huge dark cypress tree rises like a flame in the foreground. Analyze. Every part is made of thick, visible strokes that follow the forms: spirals in the sky, waves in the hills, upward flicks in the cypress. Deep blues and bright yellows set up strong contrasts. The tree links the earth to the sky. Interpret. Van Gogh painted the view from his window at Saint-Rémy, but much of it from memory and imagination; the village was changed and the sky invented. The picture expresses feeling, not a record of one night.

Van Gogh wanted color and brushwork to carry emotion directly, the way music does. He wrote that instead of trying to reproduce exactly what he saw, he used color "more arbitrarily" to express himself forcefully. Thick paint (impasto) makes every stroke visible as a trace of the painter's hand.

People think Van Gogh painted only a few pictures. He made more than 850 paintings in about ten years, and around 2,100 works in all, counting drawings and watercolors. He sold very little in his lifetime, which is a different thing from painting little.

blocks.name: ar-compare
blocks.cap: Sunflowers (A), painted in Arles in 1888, and The Bedroom (B), his room in the Yellow House, in a version of 1889.

blocks.html: In Sunflowers he painted yellow on yellow, from fresh blooms to withered seed heads, in thick paint. In The Bedroom he painted his room in Arles in flat, strong colors and tilted perspective, wanting it to suggest rest. He made three versions of it.

blocks.title: Seen or felt?
blocks.q: Van Gogh's letters say he changed the village and painted the sky partly from imagination in The Starry Night. What does that tell us about his aim?
steps: He started from a real view.
He changed it and invented parts.
So his aim was to express feeling, not to record the scene exactly.
blocks.a: He painted to express feeling, not to make an exact record.

blocks.html: Two painters who began near the Impressionists went in opposite directions after 1880. Paul Cézanne (1839 to 1906) is reported to have said he wanted to make Impressionism "something solid and lasting, like the art of museums." Paul Gauguin (1848 to 1903) wanted to leave behind the observed world for color, symbol and dream. Both opened roads into modern art. With Seurat and Van Gogh, they are called the Post-Impressionists.

blocks.text: Looking closely: The Basket of Apples

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Paul Cézanne, The Basket of Apples, about 1893. The Art Institute of Chicago.

blocks.html: Describe. On a table covered with a rumpled white cloth sit a tipped basket of apples, a bottle and a plate of biscuits, with apples spilling across the cloth. Analyze. Look at the table: its front edge does not line up on the two sides of the cloth, as if it were seen from two heights. The bottle leans; the plate of biscuits tilts up toward us, seen more from above than the basket. The apples are built of small, parallel patches of color, warm against cool, so they feel round and heavy. Interpret. Cézanne was not making mistakes. He combined what he saw from several slightly different positions and adjusted shapes so the whole picture would hold together, solid and balanced.
Paul Cézanne built landscapes and still lifes from patches of color and simple forms, a path toward Cubism; Paul Gauguin used flat, bold color and outlines.

People think Cézanne's tilted tables are mistakes. He combined several viewpoints on purpose, and bent edges and tilted objects to balance the composition. In a letter of 1904 he advised a young painter to treat nature "by the cylinder, the sphere, the cone." Picasso and Braque took that idea further in Cubism.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Paul Cézanne, Mont Sainte-Victoire, about 1902 to 1906. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York.

blocks.html: Near his home at Aix-en-Provence, Cézanne painted the mountain of Sainte-Victoire again and again, more than thirty times in oil and dozens more in watercolor. In this late view, fields, trees and houses become blocks of green, ochre and blue laid side by side, and the mountain sits on top like a solid wedge, almost as near as the fields.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Paul Gauguin, Vision after the Sermon, 1888. National Galleries of Scotland, Edinburgh.

blocks.html: In Brittany in 1888, at Pont-Aven, Gauguin painted women in white bonnets who, after a church sermon, see the Bible story of Jacob wrestling with an angel. The ground is flat, unnatural red. A tree trunk cuts diagonally across the picture, dividing the women's real world from their vision. Forms are simplified and outlined in dark lines, like stained glass or Japanese prints, a style called cloisonnism or synthetism. Gauguin spent two months with Van Gogh in Arles later that year.

Both painters stepped away from Impressionism's goal of recording a moment of light. Cézanne looked for the lasting structure under the changing surface. Gauguin chose colors for what they meant and felt, not for what the eye saw. Their two roads, structure and expressive color, led to Cubism and to Fauvism and Expressionism.

blocks.title: Mistake or method?
blocks.q: In a Cézanne still life the left and right parts of the table edge do not meet in one straight line. Explain.
steps: The cloth hides the middle of the edge.
Cézanne painted each side as seen from a slightly different position.
He adjusted forms for balance, choosing structure over a single fixed viewpoint.
blocks.a: Method: he combined viewpoints on purpose.

blocks.html: Africa is a continent of more than fifty countries and thousands of peoples, each with its own arts. In Art History I you met Nok, Ife, Benin and Great Zimbabwe. This lesson looks at arts made from the 1800s into the 1900s, many of them by peoples of West Africa, and at how they were used.

Many African masks and figures were not made to stand still in a room. They were made for performance and ceremony: a mask was worn with a full costume that hid the dancer, and it appeared with music, song and dance at farming festivals, initiations, funerals and celebrations. The carving is only one part of a whole event. The carvers were trained specialists, often blacksmiths or members of carving families, and they worked within traditions while adding their own skill and invention.
Many African masks and figures were made for performance and ceremony, seen in motion with costume, music and dance; textiles such as Asante kente carry meaning in their patterns.

blocks.text: Looking closely: a Ci Wara headdress

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Male Antelope Headdress (Ci Wara), Bamana artists, Mali, 19th century. Wood. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York.

blocks.html: Describe. A tall, slender carved wooden antelope with long, upward-curving horns, an arched neck and a zigzag openwork mane, standing on a small base. Analyze. The forms are reduced to lines and open spaces, so it looks light and graceful from the side, where it was meant to be seen. Repeated zigzags run through the mane. Interpret. Among the Bamana people of Mali, Ci Wara is the mythical being, part antelope, who taught people to farm. At planting and harvest, young men danced wearing these headdresses fixed on basketry caps, with costumes of fiber, imitating the leaps of antelopes, in male and female pairs, to honor good farmers and the work of the fields.

People judge a mask as a still object on a museum wall. Most were meant to be worn and danced, with a full costume, music and an audience, often seen from below and in motion. A museum shows only the carved part. When you look at one, imagine the costume, the movement and the occasion.

Kente cloth of the Asante people of Ghana (and of their Ewe neighbors) is woven by men on narrow horizontal looms in strips about 10 centimeters (4 inches) wide, which are then sewn edge to edge into a large cloth. Patterns of color and block designs have names, often tied to proverbs, historical events or ideas; some were once reserved for royalty. Wearing a particular pattern can say something about the wearer or the occasion.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Great Mosque of Djenné, Mali, rebuilt 1907 by builders led by master mason Ismaila Traoré (the first mosque on the site dates to the 13th century).

blocks.html: Architecture can be a shared performance too. The Great Mosque of Djenné, rebuilt in 1907, is the largest mud-brick building in the world. Wooden beams stick out of its walls; they strengthen the structure and serve as scaffolding. Because rain wears the mud away, the whole town replasters the mosque every year in a festival, with music and races to bring the mud. It is a World Heritage Site.

An object used in ceremony gets its full meaning from that use. A headdress danced at the planting season connects farming, ancestors and the community; a mosque replastered by the whole town binds the town to its building. Studying these works means studying the events and the people as well as the objects.

blocks.title: Object or event?
blocks.q: A museum shows a carved wooden mask on a stand. Its label says it was worn in funeral dances with a raffia costume. What is missing from the display?
steps: The costume that hid the dancer.
The movement of the dance, the music and the songs.
The audience and the occasion that gave the mask its meaning.
blocks.a: The costume, the performance and the occasion.

blocks.html: The Kingdom of Benin, of the Edo people, grew powerful in what is now southern Nigeria (not the modern country of Benin). Its capital, Benin City, was ruled by a divine king, the Oba. You met its early art in Art History I. From the 1500s on, its artists made some of the most famous works of African art for the royal palace.

The so-called Benin Bronzes are mostly of brass (copper alloyed with zinc), plus works in ivory and wood. A royal guild of brass casters, the Igun Eronmwon, worked only for the Oba, using the lost-wax method: a model is made in wax over a clay core, covered in clay, heated so the wax melts out, and filled with molten metal. They made memorial heads of past Obas for royal altars, and hundreds of rectangular plaques, nailed to the wooden pillars of the palace, showing the Oba, warriors, court officials, ceremonies and Portuguese traders, who arrived in the 1480s and traded the brass.
Guilds in the Kingdom of Benin (in today's Nigeria) cast brass plaques and heads for the Oba's palace from the 1500s on; British troops took thousands of these works in 1897.

blocks.text: Looking closely: a Queen Mother pendant mask

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Queen Mother Pendant Mask (Iyoba), Edo peoples, Kingdom of Benin, 16th century. Ivory, iron and copper. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York.

blocks.html: Describe. A small ivory face, about the size of a hand, with calm, wide eyes, two inlaid iron strips on the forehead, and a tall openwork crown of tiny bearded heads. Analyze. The face is smooth and idealized; the dark inlaid iron on the forehead and eyes stands out against the pale ivory. The tiny bearded heads in the crown represent Portuguese traders, linked to the sea, to wealth and to Olokun, god of the waters. Interpret. The mask is believed to show Idia, the mother of Oba Esigie, who ruled in the early 1500s; she was the first to hold the title of Queen Mother (Iyoba) and was honored for her role in her son's victories. The Oba wore such pendants at his hip in ceremonies. Ivory, white like the clay used in rituals, was a royal material.

Benin art was court art: it recorded the Oba's power, his ancestors, his officials and his ceremonies, and it was used in the rituals that kept the kingdom in order. Only the king could commission works in brass and ivory, and their style was carefully controlled, which is why they look consistent over centuries.

In 1897, after a British party traveling to Benin City was attacked and most of its members killed, a British military expedition captured the city, burned much of the palace and took thousands of works of brass, ivory and wood. Many were sold to cover the costs, and they are now in museums in Europe, North America and elsewhere, including the British Museum in London and the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York.

People think the Benin Bronzes come from the modern Republic of Benin. They come from the old Kingdom of Benin, in what is now southern Nigeria; the Republic of Benin is a different country to the west, which took its name in 1975.

blocks.title: Bronze or brass?
blocks.q: A museum label calls a Benin plaque a "bronze." Tests show it is copper mixed with zinc. What is it, and why the name?
steps: Bronze is copper with tin; brass is copper with zinc.
Most "Benin Bronzes" are in fact brass.
"Bronze" became the common name for the whole group, including some ivory and wood pieces.
blocks.a: It is brass; "Benin Bronzes" is the traditional name for the group.

blocks.html: Hundreds of Native nations lived in North America, with their own languages, beliefs and arts. In Art History I you met the Ancestral Puebloans and other ancient cultures. This lesson looks at four traditions of the 1800s and early 1900s, a time of great upheaval, when many nations were forced from their lands. Their arts continued, changed and are still made today.

On the Pacific coast of what is now British Columbia and southeast Alaska, Haida, Tlingit, Tsimshian, Kwakwaka'wakw and other nations carved tall poles from single trunks of red cedar. A pole displays a family's crests (animals and beings linked to its history, such as Raven, Eagle, Bear and Killer Whale), records events, honors the dead or welcomes guests. The carving uses a style that scholars call formline: flowing outlines that swell and narrow, ovoid shapes and U-forms, usually in black and red. Poles are not worshipped; they are more like family histories carved in wood. Cedar decays in the wet climate, so poles are recarved and replaced, as at Sitka National Historical Park in Alaska.

blocks.text: Looking closely: a Navajo chief's blanket

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Chief's Blanket, Third Phase, Navajo (Diné) weaver, about 1855 to 1865. Wool. The Art Institute of Chicago.

blocks.html: Describe. A wide wool blanket with bold horizontal stripes of black, white and dark blue, and red diamond and half-diamond shapes at the center, the corners and the middle of each side. Analyze. The design is symmetrical in both directions, so when the blanket is wrapped around the shoulders, the diamonds line up across the back and front. The weave is tight and fine. Interpret. Navajo (Diné) weaving was done by women, on upright looms. "Chief's blankets" were costly trade goods, prized by leaders of other nations such as the Ute and the peoples of the Plains, not worn only by Navajo chiefs. Collectors group them into "phases": stripes alone, then stripes with bars, then diamonds, as here.

Northwest Coast carvers made totem poles in formline style; Navajo weavers made striped blankets; Plains artists drew on ledger paper; Pueblo potters made painted and polished pottery. These are many different arts, not one style.

On the Great Plains, artists of the Lakota, Cheyenne, Kiowa and other nations had long painted brave deeds and important events on buffalo hides. As the buffalo were nearly wiped out and nations were confined to reservations, from about the 1860s artists drew with pencil, crayon and ink on the lined pages of account books, called ledger art: scenes of ceremonies, hunting, courtship and the changing world around them. In the Southwest, Pueblo potters built pots by hand from coils of clay, without a wheel. At San Ildefonso Pueblo, Maria Martinez (1887 to 1980) and her husband Julian developed a black-on-black ware around 1919: polished shiny black and matte black designs on the same pot, made by smothering the fire so smoke turned the clay black.

People speak of "Native American art" as one style. Hundreds of nations made very different arts, from cedar poles to wool blankets to drawings and pottery, with different materials, purposes and meanings, and many still do. Name the nation and the region when you describe a work.

Each art grew from its land and way of life: cedar forests on the wet Northwest Coast, sheep and wool in the Southwest after the Spanish brought sheep, buffalo and later paper on the Plains, and good clay in the Pueblo villages. Trade, new materials and hard times changed the arts again, and artists adapted.

Riders and ceremonies are typical subjects.

blocks.html: Van Gogh and Gauguin had shown that color could carry feeling and need not copy nature. Around 1905 younger painters took the next step and used color with no regard for what things "really" look like.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Henri Matisse, Woman with a Hat, 1905. San Francisco Museum of Modern Art.

blocks.html: Describe. Henri Matisse (1869 to 1954) painted his wife, Amélie, in a huge, elaborate hat, holding a fan. Analyze. Her face is streaked with green, yellow and pink; the background is patches of turquoise, pink and orange; the hat is a pile of loose, bright strokes. Nothing is smoothly blended, and much of the brushwork is left raw. Interpret. Color here builds the picture and its mood, not the description of skin and cloth. At the 1905 Salon d'Automne in Paris, critics mocked it, and the critic Louis Vauxcelles called Matisse and his friends fauves, "wild beasts." The name stuck: Fauvism. The painting was bought by the American writers Leo and Gertrude Stein.
Around 1905 the Fauves, led by Henri Matisse, used wild, unnatural color; German Expressionists such as Ernst Ludwig Kirchner and Franz Marc used color and distortion to express feeling.

People think the Fauves couldn't see real colors. They chose color for feeling and design, not description, and they could paint naturalistically when they wished (Matisse trained in the academic way). A green stripe down a face is a decision about color and structure.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: André Derain, Charing Cross Bridge, 1906. Musée d'Orsay, Paris.

blocks.html: André Derain (1880 to 1954) painted London for the dealer Ambroise Vollard in 1906: a yellow sky, an orange road, a river in green and blue. He knew Monet's misty views of the Thames and answered them with pure, hot color.

In Germany, two groups pushed color and distortion toward inner feeling. Die Brücke ("The Bridge") was founded in Dresden in 1905 by Ernst Ludwig Kirchner and fellow architecture students. In Munich in 1911 Wassily Kandinsky and Franz Marc formed Der Blaue Reiter ("The Blue Rider"), with an almanac and exhibitions. Their forerunner was the Norwegian Edvard Munch, whose The Scream (1893) turns a sunset into a cry of anxiety.

blocks.name: ar-compare
blocks.cap: Die Brücke (A): Kirchner's Street, Dresden, 1908. Der Blaue Reiter (B): Marc's The Large Blue Horses, 1911.

blocks.html: In Street, Dresden (1908), Kirchner tilted the pavement up into a pink slope and made the crowd's faces mask-like, to express the strangeness of the modern city. Franz Marc (1880 to 1916) painted animals as symbols of innocence; in The Large Blue Horses (1911) blue stands for the spiritual, in curving forms echoed by red hills.

A painting can work like music: a chord of color affects us directly, before we name what it shows. Both groups believed that color and line could carry emotion straight to the viewer, so they freed them from description. Marc, for example, gave colors meanings of his own: blue was spiritual and masculine, yellow gentle and joyful.

blocks.title: Fauve or Expressionist?
blocks.q: A 1908 painting shows a city street with mask-like faces and a tilted pink pavement, made by a painter in Dresden. Which label fits?
steps: Dresden was the home of Die Brücke.
Distortion of space and faces expresses unease about the city.
That is German Expressionism.
blocks.a: German Expressionism (Die Brücke).

blocks.html: Cézanne had built pictures from simple forms and combined several viewpoints. From about 1907 two young painters in Paris, the Spaniard Pablo Picasso (1881 to 1973) and the Frenchman Georges Braque (1882 to 1963), pushed those ideas so far that they broke with the single viewpoint that had ruled European painting since the Renaissance (see Linear Perspective). Working side by side, they created Cubism.

In 1908 Braque showed landscapes painted at L'Estaque in southern France, with houses reduced to blocky shapes. The critic Louis Vauxcelles (who had named the Fauves) mocked their "cubical oddities," and the name Cubism followed. In the first phase, Analytic Cubism (about 1909 to 1912), objects were broken into many small, overlapping facets in browns and grays, seen from several sides at once. In Synthetic Cubism (from about 1912), the artists built pictures from larger, flatter shapes, brighter color and pasted papers: in 1912 Picasso made the first collage and Braque the first papier collé (pasted paper).
Picasso and Braque, from about 1907, broke objects into facets seen from several viewpoints at once; Juan Gris and others carried Cubism on.

blocks.text: Looking closely: Juan Gris, Portrait of Pablo Picasso

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Juan Gris, Portrait of Pablo Picasso, 1912. The Art Institute of Chicago.

blocks.html: Describe. A man holding a palette, his head, neck and body built of flat, angled planes in cool blue, gray and brown. An inscription at the lower right reads "Hommage à Pablo Picasso." Analyze. Juan Gris (1887 to 1927), who had moved to Paris from Madrid in 1906, organized the figure on a grid of diagonals. Each facet is lit from its own direction; we see the face partly from the front and partly from the side. Compared with the shattered, crowded facets of early Cubism, Gris's planes are crisp, large and orderly. Interpret. It is a tribute to the leader of the movement, painted in the movement's language, and it shows a younger artist making that language clearer and more structured.

People think Cubism is about cubes. The name came from a critic's mocking remark. The idea is many viewpoints in one picture: showing an object as we know it from walking around it, its top and side, front and profile, rather than as it looks from one fixed spot at one moment.

A single viewpoint shows only one side of a thing at one instant. We know objects more fully: a glass is round at the top and straight at the side; a face has a front and a profile. Cubism puts that knowledge on the canvas. The cost is that the picture no longer looks like a window onto the world; it becomes a flat construction, and that idea opened the door to abstraction.

blocks.title: Which viewpoints?
blocks.q: A Cubist still life shows a guitar whose round sound hole appears as a full circle while its neck is seen from the side. Explain.
steps: From the front, the sound hole looks round.
The neck is best understood from the side.
The painter combined both views in one image.
blocks.a: Two viewpoints are combined: front for the sound hole, side for the neck.

blocks.html: Cubism had broken objects apart, and Fauvism and Expressionism had freed color. Between about 1910 and 1915 several artists, working separately in different countries, took the last step: paintings that show no objects at all, only color, line and shape. This is abstract (or non-objective) art.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Wassily Kandinsky, Composition VII, 1913. State Tretyakov Gallery, Moscow.

blocks.html: Describe. A large canvas, about 2 by 3 meters, crowded with bright patches, black lines, swirls and shapes in red, blue, yellow, purple and green, with no recognizable objects. Analyze. The forms seem to whirl around a dark center left of middle. Hard black lines cut across soft, cloudy color; some areas are dense, others open. Kandinsky made more than thirty studies for it and painted the final canvas in three to four days. Interpret. Kandinsky (1866 to 1944), a Russian who worked in Munich, compared painting to music: colors were like tones and chords that move the soul directly. In his book Concerning the Spiritual in Art (1911) he argued that art should express inner, spiritual truth. Scholars have traced faint echoes of themes such as floods and resurrection in the forms; Kandinsky wanted viewers to feel them rather than read them.
Between about 1910 and 1915, Wassily Kandinsky, Kazimir Malevich and others made paintings that show no objects at all, only color, line and shape.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Kazimir Malevich, Black Square, 1915. State Tretyakov Gallery, Moscow.

blocks.html: In Russia, Kazimir Malevich (1879 to 1935) went further. At the "0.10" exhibition in Petrograd in December 1915 he hung Black Square high in the corner of the room, the place where a religious icon hung in a Russian home. He called his movement Suprematism, the "supremacy of pure feeling." The original canvas is cracked; he painted later versions.

People think abstract art is random. Its makers planned color, balance and rhythm, made many studies, and often wrote long explanations of their aims: Kandinsky's book on the spiritual in art, Malevich's Suprematist manifesto, Mondrian's essays (see De Stijl). Look for the decisions: where the weight falls, which colors meet, how the eye moves.

If a painting is a flat surface arranged with color and shape, and if color affects feeling directly, then a picture does not need a subject to be meaningful. Abstraction keeps only what these artists believed mattered most. Many of them were interested in spiritual movements of the time and saw abstract art as a way to show the invisible.

Who was first is debated. Kandinsky dated an abstract watercolor to 1910, though some scholars think it was made later. The Swedish painter Hilma af Klint made abstract paintings from 1906, but showed them to very few people, and they became widely known only in the 1980s. The Czech painter František Kupka and the French painter Robert Delaunay also made abstract works around 1912. It is safest to say that abstraction arose in several places at once.

blocks.name: ar-design
blocks.cap: Abstract art is built from the principles of design: balance, rhythm and contrast.

blocks.title: Random or planned?
blocks.q: An abstract painting has a large heavy black shape at the left and several small bright red shapes scattered at the right. Is it random?
steps: The big dark shape has visual weight on one side.
Several small bright shapes balance it on the other.
That is asymmetrical balance, a planned decision.
blocks.a: Planned: it is balanced asymmetrically.

blocks.html: Two movements of the 1910s reacted to the modern world in opposite ways. The Futurists loved it; the Dada artists, after the horror of World War I, mocked it, and mocked art itself.

On February 20, 1909, the Italian poet Filippo Tommaso Marinetti published the Futurist Manifesto on the front page of the Paris newspaper Le Figaro. He praised speed, machines, cities and even war, and called for destroying museums and libraries. Painters such as Umberto Boccioni, Giacomo Balla and Carlo Carrà joined him, using the broken forms of Cubism to show motion.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Umberto Boccioni, The City Rises, 1910. Museum of Modern Art, New York.

blocks.html: Describe. A huge red horse charges across the canvas, with workers straining to hold it; behind them are scaffolding, factory chimneys and new buildings. Analyze. Everything is blurred by sweeping, curving strokes; forms melt into each other, so the eye cannot rest. The colors are hot and bright. Interpret. The horse stands for the energy of the growing industrial city. Boccioni (1882 to 1916) painted it as a hymn to progress and labor. He died in World War I, in 1916.
Italian Futurists (from 1909) glorified speed and machines; Dada artists in Zurich (from 1916) and beyond mocked art itself, as in Marcel Duchamp's Fountain (1917).

In 1916, in neutral Switzerland, the writer Hugo Ball and the performer Emmy Hennings opened the Cabaret Voltaire in Zurich. Artists and poets from countries at war, among them Tristan Tzara, Jean Arp and Sophie Taeuber, gathered there for nonsense poems, noise music, masks and collages. They took the name Dada, a nonsense word (in French a child's word for a hobbyhorse). Dada spread to Berlin, where Hannah Höch made photomontages from magazine pictures, to Paris and to New York.

In New York in 1917, Marcel Duchamp (1887 to 1968) bought a porcelain urinal from a plumbing supply store, turned it on its back, signed it "R. Mutt 1917" and submitted it, under that false name, to an exhibition that claimed to accept any work by any artist who paid the fee. The board refused to show it. Called Fountain, it is the most famous of Duchamp's readymades: ordinary manufactured objects that the artist chose and called art. The original is lost and is known from a photograph by Alfred Stieglitz; replicas were made in the 1950s and 1960s. It is still in copyright and is not shown here.

People think Dada was meant to be beautiful. It was a protest, against the war that had killed millions and against the art world's rules about skill, taste and beauty. Its weapons were nonsense, chance and provocation. Ask what question a Dada work raises, not whether it is pretty.

Duchamp's readymade asks a question that art has argued about ever since: is art made by the artist's hand, or by the artist's choice and idea? If choosing and naming an object can make it art, then the idea matters more than the craft. Many later artists built on that thought; many critics have rejected it.

blocks.title: What is the question?
blocks.q: Duchamp signed a mass-produced object with a false name and entered it in an exhibition. What question was he asking?
steps: He did not make the object; he chose it.
He entered it in an art exhibition with no jury, under a false name.
The refusal showed that the "open" show did have rules after all.
His question: who decides what counts as art, and does art require the artist's hand?
blocks.a: Who decides what art is, and whether choosing an object can make it art.

blocks.html: After World War I, many artists wanted to build a new, orderly world from the simplest parts. Two movements did this in different ways: De Stijl in the Netherlands and the Bauhaus school in Germany. Both grew out of abstraction and both wanted art to reach into everyday life: furniture, houses, typefaces and objects.

blocks.text: Looking closely: Composition with Red, Blue and Yellow

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Piet Mondrian, Composition with Red, Blue and Yellow, 1930. Kunsthaus Zürich.

blocks.html: Describe. Thick black horizontal and vertical lines divide a square canvas into rectangles. One large square at the upper right is red; a small one at the lower left is blue; a tiny one at the lower right is yellow; the rest are white. Analyze. Nothing is symmetrical, yet the picture is balanced: the heavy red is answered by the small, dense blue and yellow and by the black bars, some of which stop short of the edge. Mondrian used only the three painter's primaries, black and white. Interpret. Piet Mondrian (1872 to 1944) called his style Neoplasticism: reducing painting to its basic elements to express a universal harmony behind the changing world.
Piet Mondrian reduced painting to black lines and primary colors; the Bauhaus school in Germany (1919 to 1933) joined art, craft and industry in modern design.

People think Mondrian's grids were quick to make. He worked slowly, adjusting line widths, spacing and the size of each color for weeks or months, often moving strips of tape and repainting, until the balance felt exactly right. The simplicity is the result of many decisions.

De Stijl ("The Style") was founded in 1917 by Theo van Doesburg and Mondrian, with a magazine of the same name. The furniture maker and architect Gerrit Rietveld turned its ideas into objects: his Red and Blue Chair (designed in 1917, painted in its famous colors around 1923) and the Rietveld Schröder House in Utrecht (1924), with sliding walls and planes of primary color.

The architect Walter Gropius founded the Bauhaus in Weimar in 1919. It moved to Dessau in 1925, into a building Gropius designed with a glass curtain wall that showed the workshops inside, and to Berlin in 1932; under pressure from the Nazi government it closed in 1933. Students learned basic design, then trained in workshops (metal, weaving, furniture, printing, ceramics) to design objects that could be made by industry. Teachers included Wassily Kandinsky and Paul Klee; Anni Albers made weavings, Marianne Brandt metal lamps and teapots, Marcel Breuer tubular steel chairs. When teachers and students left Germany, many came to the United States and spread its ideas.

Industry could now make things cheaply for everyone, but most mass-produced goods imitated old handmade styles. The Bauhaus asked: what should a well-made modern object look like if it is designed for the machine? Its answer was simple forms, honest materials, no added ornament, and close work between artists and manufacturers.

blocks.name: ar-design
blocks.cap: Mondrian's balance: unequal parts weighed against each other.

blocks.title: Why is it balanced?
blocks.q: In a Mondrian, a big red square sits at the upper right, and small blue and yellow squares at the lower left and right. Why doesn't it feel lopsided?
steps: A large area of a strong color has a lot of visual weight.
Small areas of intense blue and yellow, and thick black lines, add weight elsewhere.
The unequal parts balance each other: asymmetrical balance.

blocks.html: Out of Dada's playful revolt came a movement with a program. In 1924 the French poet André Breton published the Surrealist Manifesto. Inspired by the psychologist Sigmund Freud's ideas about dreams and the unconscious mind, Breton defined Surrealism as "pure psychic automatism": expressing thought free from reason, taste and morality. The aim was to join dream and reality into a "super-reality," a surréalité.

Surrealist artists worked in two main ways. Some used automatism: drawing or painting without planning, letting the hand move freely, then developing what appeared; Joan Miró and André Masson worked this way. Others painted dream images with sharp, precise realism, so that impossible things look real: Salvador Dalí and René Magritte.

Surrealists, after André Breton's manifesto of 1924, painted dreams and the unconscious: Salvador Dalí's melting watches and René Magritte's puzzles. Their works are still in copyright, so they are described here, not shown.

blocks.text: Looking closely (in words): The Persistence of Memory

blocks.html: Salvador Dalí (1904 to 1989) painted The Persistence of Memory in 1931; it is in the Museum of Modern Art, New York, and is still in copyright. Describe. It is small, about 24 by 33 centimeters (9.5 by 13 inches). On a barren shore under a clear sky, three pocket watches hang limp and soft: one draped over a branch of a dead tree, one over the edge of a table, one over a strange, pale, sleeping form on the ground. A fourth watch, closed and orange, is covered with ants. Golden cliffs of the Catalan coast rise in the distance. Analyze. Everything is painted with tiny, smooth brushstrokes and sharp detail, like an old master, so the impossible soft watches look real. Long shadows and empty space give a dreamlike stillness. Interpret. Hard, mechanical time melts in the world of dreams and memory. Dalí said the idea came to him while looking at a soft Camembert cheese melting in the sun.

People call any odd picture "surreal." The movement had a definite aim: to free the unconscious mind, through automatism or through dream images. Many Surrealist works are painted with very precise realism. A strange picture is not Surrealist unless it comes from that program, and the word "surreal" in everyday speech is looser than the art movement.

René Magritte (1898 to 1967), a Belgian, painted puzzles about images and words. In The Treachery of Images (1929, Los Angeles County Museum of Art) a carefully painted pipe floats above the words Ceci n'est pas une pipe, "This is not a pipe." He was right: it is a painting of a pipe, not a pipe. The Swiss artist Meret Oppenheim made Object (1936), a cup, saucer and spoon covered in fur, turning a familiar thing into something unsettling.

Freud argued that much of the mind is hidden from us, and that dreams, slips of the tongue and free association reveal it. If that is true, art made by reason alone leaves out most of what we are. Surrealists tried to let that hidden part speak, either by giving up control or by painting the strange logic of dreams with total clarity.

blocks.html: Two inventions made the modern city possible: the steel frame and the safe passenger elevator. In Chicago after the great fire of 1871, architects began building tall office buildings on iron and then steel skeletons. A wall no longer had to hold up the building; it could be a thin skin hung on the frame, with big windows. (Compare the thick bearing walls of Baroque and earlier buildings.)

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Louis Sullivan and Dankmar Adler, Wainwright Building, St. Louis, Missouri, 1890 to 1891.

blocks.html: Describe. A ten-story red brick and terra-cotta office block, with a solid base of two stories, a middle of tall, closely spaced vertical piers between windows, and a deep cornice at the top covered in leafy ornament. Analyze. The piers run up without a break, stressing height, and the building reads in three parts like a classical column: base, shaft, capital. Inside, a steel frame carries the loads. Interpret. Louis Sullivan (1856 to 1924) wrote in an 1896 essay that a tall building "must be every inch a proud and soaring thing," and that "form ever follows function," which became the slogan "form follows function."

blocks.name: ar-arch
blocks.cap: A bearing wall against a steel frame: in a frame building, the walls hang on the skeleton.

blocks.html: Louis Sullivan's skyscrapers ("form follows function"), Frank Lloyd Wright's Robie House (1909 to 1910) and Fallingwater (1935 to 1939), and Art Deco towers like the Chrysler Building (1930) shaped modern American architecture.

People think a skyscraper's walls hold it up. A steel frame carries the weight; the outer walls hang on it like a curtain (a "curtain wall") and can be thin, or even mostly glass. The Wainwright's brick piers look structural, but the steel inside does the work.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Frank Lloyd Wright, Fallingwater, Mill Run, Pennsylvania, 1935 to 1939.

blocks.html: Frank Lloyd Wright (1867 to 1959), who had worked for Sullivan, designed houses that hug the land. His Prairie style houses near Chicago, like the Robie House (1909 to 1910), stretch out in long, low horizontal lines with overhanging roofs. At Fallingwater, designed in 1935 as a weekend house for the Kaufmann family of Pittsburgh, he set the house over a waterfall on Bear Run. Concrete terraces cantilever out over the stream, anchored to a stone core, so the house seems to grow from the rock.

blocks.text: Art Deco and the machine age

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: William Van Alen, Chrysler Building, New York, 1928 to 1930 (center, with the pointed spire).

blocks.html: Art Deco, named after a 1925 Paris design exhibition, used bold geometry, zigzags, sunbursts and shiny materials. The Chrysler Building (1928 to 1930), by William Van Alen, rises 1,046 feet to a stainless-steel crown of stacked arches and a needle spire; for about a year it was the tallest building in the world, until the Empire State Building opened in 1931. In Europe, Le Corbusier's Villa Savoye (1928 to 1931) and the Bauhaus pushed toward plain white boxes on slender columns, with no ornament at all.

Function and structure suggested a new beauty. If a building's frame does the work, the wall can open up to light; if its use is offices, its form can express a stack of offices. Wright added a third idea: a building should belong to its site. These ideas replaced copying historical styles.

blocks.title: Wall or frame?
blocks.q: A 1930 tower has a skin of brick and glass only a few inches thick, yet rises 77 stories. What holds it up?
steps: A wall that thin could not carry 77 stories of weight.
A steel frame inside carries the loads.
The brick and glass are a curtain wall hung on the frame.
blocks.a: Its steel frame.
