blocks.html: In 1913 the Armory Show in New York brought European modern art, from Impressionism to Cubism, before large crowds in New York, Chicago and Boston, many of them shocked. But American artists were already building a modern art of their own, encouraged by the photographer and gallery owner Alfred Stieglitz (see Photography as Modern Art), and over the next decades they found distinctly American subjects.

Georgia O'Keeffe (1887 to 1986) painted flowers so close up and so large that they fill the canvas and become almost abstract, as in Black Iris (1926, The Metropolitan Museum of Art), and later the bones, hills and skies of New Mexico. Edward Hopper (1882 to 1967) painted American cities and towns in strong, flat light: empty streets, gas stations, offices and diners. In Nighthawks (1942, The Art Institute of Chicago) three customers and a counterman sit inside a brightly lit corner diner at night, seen through a huge curved window; no door to the street is visible, and the people do not look at each other. Both paintings are still in copyright and are not shown here.

Georgia O'Keeffe painted close-up flowers and desert forms; Edward Hopper lonely city scenes; Harlem Renaissance artists such as Aaron Douglas and, later, Jacob Lawrence told Black American history. American modern art was built before the 1940s.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Grant Wood, American Gothic, 1930. Oil on beaverboard. The Art Institute of Chicago.

blocks.html: Describe. A stern farmer holding a pitchfork stands beside a woman in front of a white wooden farmhouse with a pointed Gothic window in its gable. Analyze. Everything is painted with crisp, smooth precision. The vertical lines repeat: the pitchfork's tines echo in the stitching of the man's overalls, the window's arch and the long faces. The figures are close to us, frontal and still. Interpret. Grant Wood (1891 to 1942) saw the house in Eldon, Iowa, and posed his sister Nan and his dentist for the figures. Wood and his sister described them as a farmer and his daughter, though many viewers have taken them for a married couple. Critics have argued since 1930 whether it gently satirizes small-town Midwesterners or honors them; Wood said he meant it as a tribute. It is part of Regionalism, a movement of the 1930s that painted rural America.

People think American art followed Europe until the 1940s. O'Keeffe, Hopper, the Regionalists and the artists of the Harlem Renaissance built a distinctly American modern art in the 1910s, 1920s and 1930s. The later fame of New York painting (see Abstract Expressionism) grew from that ground.

In the 1920s and 1930s Harlem, in New York, was the center of a flowering of Black American writing, music and art. The painter Aaron Douglas (1899 to 1979) illustrated books and magazines and painted murals in a style of flat, layered silhouettes, with rings of light and rhythms borrowed from jazz and from African art; his 1934 murals for the New York Public Library, now at the Schomburg Center for Research in Black Culture, trace history from Africa to Harlem. The sculptor Augusta Savage taught many young artists. One of them, Jacob Lawrence (1917 to 2000), painted The Migration Series (1940 to 1941): 60 small panels in flat, bright colors telling the story of the Great Migration of more than a million Black Americans from the rural South to northern cities. The Museum of Modern Art owns the odd-numbered panels and The Phillips Collection the even-numbered ones. These works are in copyright and are described here.

Artists in each region and community turned to the life they knew: O'Keeffe to the desert, Hopper to the city, Wood to Iowa, Douglas and Lawrence to the history and experience of Black Americans. Modern styles, such as flat color, simplified forms and strong design, became ways to tell American stories.

blocks.title: Father or husband?
blocks.q: Viewers argue whether the pair in American Gothic are husband and wife or father and daughter. How should a careful description handle this?
steps: Grant Wood and his sister, who posed for the woman, described them as a farmer and his daughter.
Many viewers have read them as a married couple.
A careful description reports the artist's statement and notes that viewers differ.
blocks.a: Give Wood's description (father and daughter) and note that many viewers see a married couple.

blocks.html: The Mexican Revolution (1910 to 1920) overturned Mexico's old order. Afterward, the government wanted art that every citizen could see, including people who could not read. From 1921 the education minister, José Vasconcelos, gave artists the walls of public buildings: schools, ministries and the National Palace. Mexican muralism was born. It looked back to the great art of ancient Mexico and to the frescoes of the Italian Renaissance, painted in true fresco on wet plaster.

Three painters, called los tres grandes, "the three great ones," led the movement. Diego Rivera (1886 to 1957) painted crowded, colorful murals of Mexican history, from the ancient Aztec world to modern workers, most famously on the stairway and walls of the National Palace in Mexico City (from 1929 to 1935). He also painted murals in the United States, in San Francisco, Detroit and New York. José Clemente Orozco (1883 to 1949) painted darker, more tragic murals about suffering and the human condition. David Alfaro Siqueiros (1896 to 1974) experimented with industrial paints, spray guns and dramatic, swooping viewpoints. All their murals are still in copyright, so they are described here, not shown.
After the Mexican Revolution, Diego Rivera, José Clemente Orozco and David Alfaro Siqueiros painted public murals of Mexican history; Frida Kahlo painted mostly small, personal self-portraits.

Frida Kahlo (1907 to 1954) was badly injured at 18, in 1925, when a bus she was riding collided with a streetcar; she began to paint while recovering in bed, with a mirror above her. Of her roughly 140 paintings, about a third (some 55) are self-portraits. She married Diego Rivera in 1929. Her style drew on Mexican folk art and on small devotional paintings on tin called retablos: bright colors, flat backgrounds, clear outlines and symbolic objects. She often wore the long embroidered dresses of the Tehuana women of southern Mexico, to celebrate Mexican tradition.

blocks.text: Looking closely (in words): Frieda and Diego Rivera

blocks.html: Kahlo's double portrait Frieda and Diego Rivera (1931, San Francisco Museum of Modern Art) is in copyright and is described here. Describe. The couple stand hand in hand against a plain background: Rivera large and heavy in a dark suit, holding a palette and brushes; Kahlo small, in a long green dress and red shawl, her feet tiny beneath her skirt. A dove above them carries a ribbon with an inscription. Analyze. The difference in size, the flat colors and the ribbon recall Mexican folk portraits. Interpret. It is a wedding portrait in folk style, painted in San Francisco while Rivera worked on murals there; he holds the tools of the artist, and she, at this point, does not.

People think Frida Kahlo was a muralist. She painted mostly small self-portraits and personal scenes, often on board or metal; her husband, Diego Rivera, painted the huge public murals. Their art was very different in scale and purpose, public history for him, personal experience for her.

A mural reaches everyone who walks by, and a fresco becomes part of the building, lasting as long as the wall. For a government that wanted to teach a shared history after a revolution, public walls were the ideal canvas. A small self-portrait does something else: it speaks from one life to one viewer.

blocks.title: Mural or easel painting?
blocks.q: A painting about 100 by 80 centimeters shows the artist in a Tehuana dress with symbolic objects around her. Is it a Rivera mural?
steps: Murals are painted on walls and are usually huge.
This is a small self-portrait on a portable support.
The Tehuana dress and self-portrait suggest Frida Kahlo.
blocks.a: No: it is a small easel painting, most likely by Kahlo.

blocks.html: By 1900 cameras were cheap and easy (Kodak's slogan was "You press the button, we do the rest"), and millions of people took snapshots. Some photographers asked whether photography could be an art as serious as painting. Others used it to show the public truths it had not seen. Both paths grew from the early photography of Daguerre, Talbot and Cameron.

In New York, Alfred Stieglitz (1864 to 1946) led the fight for photography as art. He founded the Photo-Secession in 1902, published the magazine Camera Work, and ran a gallery known as "291," where he showed both photographs and modern painting, including some of the first American showings of Picasso and the work of Georgia O'Keeffe, whom he later married.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Alfred Stieglitz, The Steerage, 1907. Photogravure. Many prints, for example The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

blocks.html: Describe. On an ocean liner, passengers crowd the lower, cheapest deck (the steerage) and an upper deck, divided by a white gangway; a man in a straw hat leans on the rail above. Analyze. Stieglitz saw the scene as shapes: the diagonal of the gangway, the round straw hat, the funnel, the stairway, the slanting mast. He said he saw "a picture of shapes" and ran for his camera. Interpret. It is a picture of modern life and of class, upper deck and lower, and also a composition as ordered as a painting. Stieglitz published it in Camera Work in 1911 and considered it one of his best photographs.
Alfred Stieglitz fought for photography as art (The Steerage, 1907); Dorothea Lange's Migrant Mother (1936) made the Great Depression visible.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Dorothea Lange, Migrant Mother, 1936. Library of Congress (Farm Security Administration collection).

blocks.html: In the 1930s the U.S. government's Farm Security Administration hired photographers, among them Dorothea Lange (1895 to 1965) and Walker Evans, to record rural poverty during the Great Depression and build support for aid. In March 1936 Lange stopped at a pea pickers' camp near Nipomo, California, where crops had failed. She made a series of exposures of a mother and her children, moving closer each time. In the best known, the mother looks off into the distance, one hand at her chin; two children turn their faces into her shoulders and a baby sleeps on her lap. The photograph appeared in newspapers, and the government sent food to the camp. The mother, Florence Owens Thompson, was identified decades later; she said she was never paid and wished the picture had not made her a symbol.

People think a documentary photo is unposed and unchosen. Photographers choose the moment, the frame, how close to stand, and which print to show; Lange made several exposures and moved closer each time, and she had a distracting thumb removed from the negative of the famous version. A documentary photograph is truthful evidence and also a composed picture. Ask what was chosen.

A photograph seems to show the world directly, which gives it great power as evidence. But every photograph is made by someone standing somewhere, at a certain moment, with a purpose. Knowing that does not make documentary photographs false; it makes us better readers of them.

blocks.title: What was chosen?
blocks.q: Lange's camp series includes six exposures, from a distance to close up. Why does the close-up become famous?
steps: Moving closer removes distractions and fills the frame with faces and hands.
The children turning away put all the focus on the mother's face.
Lange chose which exposure to release, and she chose this one.
blocks.a: Because of the photographer's choices of distance, framing and which print to show.

blocks.html: During and after World War II, many European artists fled to New York, and a group of American painters there, building on Surrealist automatism, abstraction and American modernism, made huge abstract paintings that seemed to express inner states directly. They were called the Abstract Expressionists, or the New York School. Their works are still in copyright, so they are described here, not shown.

Critics saw two tendencies. Action painting, a term coined by the critic Harold Rosenberg in 1952, stressed the painter's gesture: the canvas as "an arena in which to act." Color field painting spread large areas of color to create a calm, absorbing space.

Jackson Pollock (1912 to 1956) painted Autumn Rhythm (Number 30) in 1950; it is in The Metropolitan Museum of Art. Describe. It is huge, about 2.7 by 5.3 meters (8.75 by 17.25 feet). Over a bare, tan canvas run webs of black, white and brown lines, loops, drips and splatters, from edge to edge, with no center and no object. Analyze. Pollock laid the canvas on the floor and moved around it, pouring and flinging enamel paint from cans, sticks and hardened brushes. The lines vary from thick puddles to whip-thin threads; the black lines make a rhythm over which white and brown are woven. Because the pattern is "all-over," the eye travels without resting. Interpret. The painting is a record of motion, like a dance written in paint, and the title suggests its autumn colors and rhythm. Photographs and a film made by Hans Namuth in 1950 show Pollock at work.
In New York after World War II, Jackson Pollock dripped paint on canvas laid on the floor (action painting), and Mark Rothko painted glowing fields of color (color field).

People say "my kid could do that." Pollock's pours were controlled and practiced: he chose paints, thinned them to the right flow, varied speed and height, and knew when to stop; films show steady, deliberate movement. Rothko built his color in many thin layers, so the edges glow and seem to float. Try it yourself and the difference appears quickly.

Mark Rothko (1903 to 1970) painted large canvases with two or three soft-edged rectangles of color floating one above another on a colored ground, as in No. 61 (Rust and Blue) (1953, Museum of Contemporary Art, Los Angeles). He wanted viewers to stand close, so that the color would surround them, and he spoke of the paintings as expressing basic human emotions. Other members of the group included Lee Krasner, who was married to Pollock; Franz Kline, with his huge black-and-white strokes; and Helen Frankenthaler, who in Mountains and Sea (1952) poured thinned paint that soaked into unprimed canvas, a soak-stain method that led to later color field painting.

After a war that had shown the worst of what people could do, many of these painters felt that familiar images were exhausted. They looked for a direct language of gesture and color, often on a scale that surrounds the viewer. The huge size is part of the meaning: you are inside the painting's space, not looking at a small window.

Recognizing a style is like recognizing a friend's handwriting: not by one letter but by a set of habits. Each period has telltale clues you can look for, in its forms, its colors, its brushwork and its subjects. Names and famous works help, but clues let you read a work you have never seen before.

blocks.html: Each period has telltale signs: Gothic pointed arches, Renaissance balance, Baroque drama, Rococo pastels, Neoclassical clarity, Impressionist strokes, Cubist facets. Read the clues, not just the famous names.

Artists of a period shared training, materials, patrons and ideas, so their works share habits. A Baroque painter trained after Caravaggio learned strong light and dark; a Neoclassical painter trained in an academy that prized clear outline. That is why a set of clues points to a period even when the artist is unknown.

blocks.html: A sets three brothers in a shallow, stage-like hall, with hard outlines, sober color and a story of duty: the clues of Neoclassicism. B sets one figure, seen from behind, before an endless sea of fog, with soft, atmospheric color and no story but a feeling: the clues of Romanticism. Both are by trained European painters within about thirty years, but their aims are opposite, and the clues show it.

People recognize styles by famous names only: "It's a Monet, so it's Impressionist." That fails as soon as you meet an unfamiliar work. Look for the visual clues: the light, the brushwork, the composition, the subject. Then check: do several clues agree? One clue alone can mislead, because styles overlap and artists borrow.

blocks.title: Read the clues
blocks.q: An unfamiliar painting shows a pastel-colored garden party, with silk dresses, soft feathery trees and playful couples. Which style?
steps: Pastel color: Rococo.
Elegant leisure and courtship: Rococo.
Soft, light handling, no deep shadow or moral message: Rococo, not Baroque or Neoclassical.
blocks.a: Rococo: three clues agree.

blocks.html: Many works reach museums with no date, no signature and no records. Art historians date them the way detectives solve a case: by gathering clues and seeing where they agree. In Telling the Styles Apart you used style clues to name a period. Here you will use several kinds of clues together to narrow a date, as in Dating and Attribution.

items: Style: brushwork, color, composition and the clues of each period.
Subject: what people chose to paint, such as railway stations (after the 1830s) or factory chimneys.
Clothes and hair: fashions changed fast and can date a portrait within a decade or two.
Materials and technique: the canvas, the support, the pigments, the printing method.
Things in the picture: a building known to be finished in a certain year, a ship, a kind of carriage.
Documents, when they exist: letters, inventories, exhibition catalogs.

blocks.html: Clothes, subject, technique, materials and style narrow a work's date before any document is found. Several clues together give a safer date than any one.

Each clue sets limits. A pigment cannot appear before it was invented, and a building cannot appear before it was built: these give an "earliest possible" date (scholars use the Latin term terminus post quem, "the limit after which"). An exhibition record gives a "latest possible" date (terminus ante quem, "the limit before which"). Style and fashion then place the work within that window.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Élisabeth Vigée Le Brun, Marie Antoinette with a Rose, 1783. Palace of Versailles.

blocks.html: Suppose this portrait had no label. Clothes and hair: towering powdered hair with feathers and a silk gown with lace were the court fashion of the late 1770s and early 1780s. Style: soft pastel color, a smooth idealized face and an easy, elegant pose are late Rococo. Sitter: if we recognize the queen of France, she was queen from 1774 until the monarchy fell in 1792. The clues agree on about 1775 to 1790; the catalog date is 1783.

People rely on one clue. Clothing can be old-fashioned on purpose (The Blue Boy wears the dress of the 1630s, painted about 1770); an artist can work in an old style; a late copy can repeat an early design. Several clues together give a safer date. If they disagree, look for the explanation.

blocks.title: Earliest possible date
blocks.q: A Japanese woodblock print of a wave uses a deep, strong Prussian blue. Prussian blue was invented in Europe in the early 1700s and reached wide use in Japanese prints around 1830. What does that suggest?
steps: The pigment gives an earliest possible date: not before it was available in Japan in quantity.
Strong Prussian blue in ukiyo-e is typical from about 1830.
So the print most likely dates from about 1830 or later, and style and subject can narrow it further.
blocks.a: About 1830 or later.

blocks.title: Combining clues
blocks.q: A photograph shows a street with a steel-framed office tower and people in long skirts and bowler hats. What can you say about its date?
steps: Photography: after 1839.
Steel-framed office towers: after the 1880s.
Long skirts and bowler hats: fashions of roughly the 1880s to the 1910s.
The window where all clues agree: about 1885 to 1915.
blocks.a: About 1885 to 1915.

blocks.html: Comparison is the art historian's most useful tool. Set two works side by side and each shows what is special about the other: you see Vermeer's quiet better next to Caravaggio's drama. Art history exams and essays often ask for it. A good comparison follows the steps of formal analysis (describe, analyze, interpret) for both works at once.

items: Subject: what does each show? Who are the figures? What is happening?
Composition: how is each arranged? Centered or off-center, calm or diagonal, deep or shallow?
Color and light: warm or cool, bright or dark, a spotlight or even light?
Technique and medium: smooth or visible strokes, oil or tempera, print or painting?
Context and purpose: who made it, for whom, when and where, and how was it used?

blocks.html: Set side by side, both paintings give dignity to women's work and both use strong, simple shapes. But the Milkmaid is calm, enclosed and timeless, a single act of care in a quiet room; the Gleaners is a social picture, in which the rich harvest far behind sharpens the poverty of the women in front. The comparison shows how two artists two centuries apart turned similar subjects to very different purposes.

The mind notices differences. A single work can look "natural," as if it could not have been made any other way. Next to another work, every choice, of light, of distance, of color, becomes visible as a choice. That is why museums often hang contrasting works together.

People describe one work and then the other, in two separate paragraphs. That is two descriptions, not a comparison. A good comparison sets them against each other point by point: "Vermeer's light comes from a window and falls on one figure; Millet's low evening light spreads across a whole field." Every sentence should mention both works.
